It is also said that it has sixty-two verses. It is also said that the whole Surah is Medinan. The correct view is that it is Meccan, because of what Ibn Mas'ud narrated, that he said: "It is the first Surah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proclaimed openly in Mecca." In al-Bukhari, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, the Prophet ﷺ prostrated during (the recitation of) al-Najm, and the Muslims, the polytheists, the jinn and the humans prostrated with him. And on the authority of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), that the Prophet ﷺ recited the Surah of al-Najm and prostrated for it, and no one among the people remained except that he prostrated. A man from the people took a handful of pebbles or dust and raised it to his face and said: "This is enough for me." Abdullah said: "I later saw him killed as a disbeliever." (Agreed upon.) The man is said to have been Umayyah ibn Khalaf. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Zayd ibn Thabit (may Allah be pleased with him), that he recited to the Prophet ﷺ the Surah "By the star when it sets" and he did not prostrate. The discussion of this has already passed at the end of al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 357], and praise be to Allah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the star when it descends. Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred. Nor does he speak from (his own) desire. It is not but a revelation revealed. He has been taught by one mighty in power, possessing strength; and he stood poised, while he was in the highest horizon. Then he approached and descended, and was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer. So He revealed to His servant what He revealed.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the star when it descends﴾. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: the meaning of "By the star when it descends" is: by the Pleiades when they set at dawn. The Arabs call the Pleiades a star, although in number they are stars. It is said that they are seven stars, six of which are visible and one of which is hidden, by which people test their eyesight. In al-Shifa' by al-Qadi Iyad, it is recorded that the Prophet ﷺ used to see eleven stars in the Pleiades. Also on the authority of Mujahid, the meaning is: by the Qur'an when it is sent down, because it was sent down in parts (nujum). This is also the view of al-Farra'. On his authority also: it means all the stars of the sky when they set. This is the view of al-Hasan, who said: Allah swore by the stars when they set. There is nothing to prevent that a single word be used for it while its meaning is plural, as in the saying of al-Ra'i:

"So she spent the night counting the stars in a place of shelter, / Swift in the hands of those who eat its stiffness."

And Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

"The most beautiful of the stars in the sky is the Pleiades, / And the Pleiades on earth is the adornment of women."

Al-Hasan also said: the intended meaning of "the star" is the stars when they fall on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Suddi said: "the star" here is Venus, because a people among the Arabs used to worship it. It is also said: the intended meaning is the stars by which the devils are pelted. The cause of this is that when Allah, exalted is He, intended to send Muhammad ﷺ as a Messenger, the falling of the stars increased before his birth. Most of the Arabs were alarmed by them and went to a soothsayer among them who was blind and used to inform them of events. They asked him about them, and he said: "Look at the twelve constellations (buruj). If any of them falls, it is the end of the world; and if none of them falls, then a great matter will happen in the world." So they sensed that. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, he was the great matter they had sensed. Then Allah, exalted is He, sent down: "By the star when it descends," meaning: that star which descended is for this prophethood which has come about. It is also said: the star here is the plant that has no stalk, and "descends" means it fell to the ground. Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them) said: "By the star" means Muhammad ﷺ, "when it descends" means when he came down from the sky on the night of the Mi'raj. On the authority of Urwah ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with both of them): that Utbah ibn Abi Lahab, who was married to a daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, intended to go out to Syria and said: "I will certainly go to Muhammad and harm him." He came to him and said: "O Muhammad, I disbelieve in 'the star when it descends' and in 'He who drew near and descended.'" Then he spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and returned his daughter to him and divorced her. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, set against him a dog from among Your dogs." Abu Talib was present, and he was distressed by it and said: "How needless you were, nephew, of this supplication!" So Utbah returned to his father and informed him. Then they set out for Syria and stopped at a station, and a monk from the monastery looked down upon them and said to them: "This is a land of predators." Abu Lahab said to his companions: "Help us, O company of Quraysh, this night! For I fear for my son from the supplication of Muhammad." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around them, and they surrounded Utbah. The lion came sniffing at their faces until it struck Utbah and killed him. Hassan said:

"Whoever returns this year to his people, / The one devoured by the beast will not return."

The origin of "najm" is rising. It is said: the tooth (najama) appeared, and so-and-so rose (najama) in the lands of such-and-such, meaning he rebelled against the authority. And "hawa" is descending and falling. It is said: hawa yahwi huwiyyan, like mada yamdi mudiyyan. Zuhayr said:

"He broke open the rough stony ground with her, and she was descending, / Descending like a bucket whose rope has let it go."

And another said [the speaker is Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, who was travelling to Syria; when he reached al-Balakath (with a thaa), he remembered his wife, for whom he was passionate, so he turned back and said these verses; after the two verses:]:

"I said, 'Here I am' when longing called me to you, / And when the drivers urged on the camels."

"While we were at al-Balakath, and al-Qa'[?] swiftly, / And the camels were descending in descent."

"A thought passed over the heart from remembering you, / Weakly, and I was not able to go on."

Al-Asma'i said: hawa, with a fatha, yahwi huwiyyan, meaning it fell downward. He said: and likewise inhawa in the journey when he proceeds in it; hawa and inhawa in it are two dialects with the same meaning, and the poet combined both in his saying:

"And how many a dwelling, had I not been there, would have been brought down / As (a thing) falls by its bulk from the summit of a steep cliff, descending."

It is also said of love: hawiya with a kasra, yahwa hawan, meaning he loved.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your companion has not strayed﴾. This is the answer to the oath, meaning: Muhammad ﷺ has not strayed from the truth, nor deviated from it.

﴿Nor has he erred﴾. Al-ghayy is the opposite of guidance, meaning he has not become misguided. It is also said: meaning he has not spoken falsehood. It is also said: meaning he has not failed in what he sought, and al-ghayy is failure. The poet said [the speaker is al-Mirqash]:

"Whoever attains good, people praise his affair, / And whoever goes astray will not lack blame for his error."

That is: whoever fails in his pursuit, people blame him. Then it is permissible that this is a report about what came after the revelation. It is also permissible that it is a general report about his states, meaning he was always one who affirmed the oneness of Allah. This is the correct view, as we have explained in al-Shura [see vol. 16, p. 55], at His saying: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from (his own) desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾. In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from (his own) desire﴾. Qatadah said: nor does he speak the Qur'an out of his own desire; ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ to him. It is also said: "from (his own) desire" means "by desire." Abu Ubaydah said: like His saying: ﴿ask about it an expert﴾, meaning, ask about it. Al-Nahhas said: Qatadah's view is better, and "from" (ʿan) is kept in its proper sense, meaning his speech does not go out from his opinion; it is only by revelation from Allah, mighty and majestic, because after it comes: ﴿It is not but a revelation revealed﴾.

The second: This verse may be used as evidence by those who do not permit the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to exercise ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in new matters. In it there is also an indication that the Sunnah (prophetic practice) is like the revelation sent down in terms of acting upon it. The hadith of al-Miqdam ibn Ma'di Karib has already passed in the introduction to the book in this regard [see vol. 1, p. 37], and praise be to Allah. Al-Sijistani said: if you wish, you may make "It is not but a revelation revealed" a substitution (badal) for "Your companion has not strayed." Ibn al-Anbari said: this is an error, because the light "in" cannot be a substitute for "ma." The evidence for this is that you do not say: "By Allah, I did not stand, in I am sitting."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has been taught by one mighty in power﴾. He means Jibril, peace be upon him, according to the view of all the commentators, except al-Hasan, who said: it is Allah, mighty and majestic. According to al-Hasan's view, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿one possessing strength﴾ is a complete sentence, and its meaning is "one possessing power," and power is among the attributes of Allah, exalted is He. Its origin is from the strong twisting of a rope, as though the twisting continued until it reached a point where untying it became difficult. Then He said: ﴿and he stood poised﴾, meaning Allah, mighty and majestic, that is, He rose over the Throne. This meaning is narrated from al-Hasan. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Farra' said: ﴿and he stood poised, while he was in the highest horizon﴾, meaning Jibril and Muhammad stood poised, peace be upon them both. This is on the basis of coordination (ʿatf) upon the pronoun in the nominative attached to "huwa." When the Arabs want to coordinate in a case like this, they make the pronoun of the coordinated noun explicit, so they say: "He and so-and-so stood up," and they rarely say "stood up and so-and-so." Al-Farra' recited:

"Do you not see that the nab' tree makes its wood hard, / And the crushed castor does not stand (equal)?"

That is: the nab' does not equal the castor, and a parallel to this is: ﴿When we are dust, and our fathers?﴾ meaning: when we and our fathers are dust. The meaning of the verse is: Jibril, he and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, stood poised on the night of the Isra' in the highest horizon.

He permitted coordination upon the pronoun so that it would not be repeated. Al-Zajjaj rejected this except in cases of poetic necessity. It is also said: the meaning is "Jibril stood poised in the highest horizon," and this is better. If the one who stood poised is Jibril, then the meaning of "possessing strength" in his description is: possessing good speech, said by Ibn Abbas. Qatadah said: possessing a tall and good form. It is also said: it means possessing soundness of body and freedom from afflictions, and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Charity is not lawful for the wealthy, nor for one who possesses sound strength." (al-sawiyy: the one with sound limbs.) Imru' al-Qays said:

"I was always among them one possessing cunning, / Firm in strength, trusted in bonds."

It is also said: "possessing strength" means possessing power. Al-Kalbi said: among Jibril's strength, peace be upon him, was that he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the lowest earth, carried them on his wing until he raised them to the sky, so that the people of the sky heard the barking of their dogs and the crowing of their roosters, and then he overturned them. Among his strength also: he saw Iblis speaking to Isa, peace be upon him, on one of the crags of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India. Among his strength was his cry to Thamud, with their number and their multitude, so they became prostrate and extinguished. Among his strength was his descent from the sky upon the prophets and his ascent to it in less time than the blink of an eye. Qutrub said: the Arabs say of every man of firm judgment and sound intellect: "possessing strength." The poet said:

"I was before meeting you one possessing strength, / With me, for every disputant, is his balance."

Wa-kāna min jazālati raʾyihi wa-ḥaṣāfati ʿaqlihi: anna Allāh ītamanahu ʿalā waḥyihi ilā jamīʿi rusulihi. Qāla al-Jawharī: wa-l-mirratu iḥdā l-ṭabāʾiʿi l-arbaʿ, wa-l-mirratu al-quwwatu wa-shiddatu al-ʿaql ayḍan. Wa-rajulun marīrun, ayy qawiyyun dhū mirratin. Qāla:

Tarā l-rajula l-naḥīfa fa-tazdarīhi ... wa-ḥashwu thiyābihi asadun marīr [[Qā'iluhu al-ʿAbbās ibn Mirdās. Wa-fī al-Tāj: wa-fī athwābihi rajulun muzayyir, bi-l-zāy. Wa-yurwā: asadun muzayyir. Wa-l-muzayyir ka-amīrin al-shadīdu al-qalb al-qawī al-nāfidhu fī l-umūr.]]

Wa-qāla Luqayṭ:

Ḥattā istamarrat ʿalā shazrin marīratuhu ... murru al-ʿazīmati lā ratā wa-lā ḍarʿā

Wa-qāla Mujāhid wa-Qatāda: (dhū mirratin) dhū quwwatin, wa-minhu qawlu Khufāf ibn Nadba:

Innī imruʾun dhū mirratin fa-istabqinī ... fīmā yanūbu mina l-khuṭūbi ṣalību

Fa-l-quwwatu takūnu min ṣifati Allāh ʿazza wa-jalla, wa-min ṣifati l-makhlūq.

(Fa-istawā) yaʿnī Jibrīla ʿalā mā bayyannā, ayy irtafaʿa wa-ʿalā ilā makānin fī l-samāʾi baʿda an ʿallama Muḥammadan (ﷺ), qālahu Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab wa-Ibn Jubayr. Wa-qīla: (fa-istawā) ayy qāma fī ṣūratihi allatī khalaqahu Allāh taʿālā ʿalayhā, li-annahu kāna yaʾtī ilā al-Nabiyyi (ﷺ) fī ṣūrati l-ādamiyyīna kamā kāna yaʾtī ilā al-anbiyāʾ, fa-sa'alahu al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) an yurīhu nafsahu allatī jabalahu Allāh ʿalayhā, fa-arāhu nafsahu marratayn: marratan fī l-arḍi wa-marratan fī l-samāʾ. Fa-ammā fī l-arḍi fa-fī al-ufuqi al-aʿlā, wa-kāna al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) bi-Ḥirāʾ, fa-ṭalaʿa lahu Jibrīlu min al-mashriqi fa-sadda al-arḍa ilā al-maghribi, fa-kharra al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) maghshiyyan ʿalayhi. Fa-nazala ilayhi fī ṣūrati l-ādamiyyīna wa-ḍammahu ilā ṣadrihi, wa-jaʿala yamsaḥu l-ghubāra ʿan wajhihi, fa-lammā afāqa al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) qāla: (Yā Jibrīlu, mā ẓanantu anna Allāha khalaqa aḥadan ʿalā mithli hādhihi l-ṣūrati). Fa-qāla: Yā Muḥammadu, innamā nashartu janāḥayni min ajniḥatī, wa-inna lī sittamiʾati janāḥin, saʿatu kulli janāḥin mā bayna l-mashriqi wa-l-maghrib. Fa-qāla: (Inna hādhā la-ʿaẓīmun). Fa-qāla: wa-mā anā fī janbi mā khalaqahu Allāh illā yasīran, wa-laqad khalaqa Allāhu Isrāfīla lahu sittumiʾati janāḥin, kullu janāḥin minhā qadra jamīʿi ajniḥatī, wa-innahu la-yataḍāʾalu aḥyānan min makhāfati Allāhi taʿālā ḥattā yakūna bi-qadri al-waṣaʿ, yaʿnī al-ʿuṣfūra al-ṣaghīr, dalīluhu qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Wa-laqad raʾāhu bi-l-ufuqi l-mubīn﴾ [[Rājiʿ j. 19 ṣ. 239]] Wa-ammā fī l-samāʾi fa-ʿinda sidrati l-muntahā, wa-lam yarahu aḥadun mina l-anbiyāʾ ʿalā tilka l-ṣūrati illā Muḥammadan (ﷺ). Wa-qawlun thālithun anna maʿnā (fa-istawā) ayy istawā l-Qurʾānu fī ṣadrihi. Wa-fīhi ʿalā hādhā wajhān: aḥaduhumā fī ṣadri Jibrīla ḥīna nazala bihi ʿalayhi. Al-thānī fī ṣadri Muḥammadin (ﷺ) ḥīna nazala ʿalayhi. Wa-qawlun rābiʿun anna maʿnā (fa-istawā) fa-iʿtadala, yaʿnī Muḥammadan (ﷺ). Wa-fīhi ʿalā hādhā wajhān: aḥaduhumā fa-iʿtadala fī quwwatihi. Al-thānī fī risālatihi. Dhakaranhumā al-Māwardī. Qultu: wa-ʿalā al-awwali yakūnu tamāmu l-kalāmi (dhū mirratin), wa-ʿalā al-thānī (shadīdu l-quwā). Wa-qawlun khāmisun anna maʿnāhu fa-irtafaʿa. Wa-fīhi ʿalā hādhā wajhān: aḥaduhumā annahu Jibrīlu ʿalayhi l-salāmu irtafaʿa ilā makānihi ʿalā mā dhakarnā ānifan. Al-thānī annahu al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) irtafaʿa bi-l-miʿrāj. Wa-qawlun sādisun (fa-istawā) yaʿnī Allāha ʿazza wa-jalla, ayy istawā ʿalā l-ʿarshi ʿalā qawli al-Ḥasan. Wa-qad maḍā al-qawlu fīhi fī (al-Aʿrāf) [[Rājiʿ j. 7 ṣ. 219 wa-j. 1 ṣ. (254)]].

Qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Wa-huwa bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā﴾ jumlatun fī mawḍiʿi l-ḥāl, wa-l-maʿnā fa-istawā ʿāliyan, ayy istawā Jibrīlu ʿāliyan ʿalā ṣūratihi, wa-lam yakun al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) qabla dhālika yarāhu ʿalayhā ḥattā sa'alahu iyyāhā ʿalā mā dhakarnā. Wa-l-ufuqu nāḥiyatu l-samāʾi wa-jamʿuhu āfāq. Wa-qāla Qatāda: huwa al-mawḍiʿu alladhī taʾtī minhu al-shams. Wa-kadhā qāla Sufyān: huwa al-mawḍiʿu alladhī taṭlaʿu minhu al-shams. Wa-naḥwuhu ʿan Mujāhid. Wa-yuqālu: ufqun wa-ufuqun mithla ʿusrun wa-ʿusurun. Wa-qad maḍā fī (Ḥā Mīm al-Sajda) [[Rājiʿ j. 15 ṣ. (374)]]. Wa-farasun ufqun bi-l-ḍammi ayy rāʾiʿun, wa-kadhālika l-unthā, qāla al-shāʿir:

Urajjilu limmatī wa-ajurru dhayla ... wa-taḥmilu shikkatī ufqun kumayt [[Qā'iluhu ʿAmr ibn Qanʿās al-Murrī. Wa-l-shikkatu al-silāḥ. Wa-fī al-Lisān: wa-taḥmilu bizzatī. Wa-l-kumaytu min al-khayli mā khalaṭa ḥumratahu sawādun ghayru khālis.]]

Wa-qīla: (wa-huwa) ayy al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) (bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā) yaʿnī laylata al-Isrāʾ, wa-hādhā ḍaʿīf, li-annahu yuqālu: istawā huwa wa-fulānun, wa-lā yuqālu istawā wa-fulānun illā fī ḍarūrati al-shiʿr. Wa-l-ṣaḥīḥu istawā Jibrīlu ʿalayhi l-salām wa-Jibrīlu bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā ʿalā ṣūratihi l-aṣliyya, li-annahu kāna yatamaththalu lil-Nabiyyi (ﷺ) idhā nazala bi-l-waḥyi fī ṣūrati rajulin, fa-aḥabba al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) an yarāhu ʿalā ṣūratihi l-ḥaqīqiyya, fa-istawā fī ufuqi l-mashriqi fa-malaʾa al-ufuq.

Qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Thumma dana fa-tadallā﴾ ayy dana Jibrīlu baʿda istiwāʾihi bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā mina l-arḍ, (fa-tadallā) fa-nazala ʿalā al-Nabiyyi (ﷺ) bi-l-waḥy. Al-maʿnā annahu lammā raʾā al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ) min ʿaẓamatihi mā raʾā, wa-hālahu dhālika, raddahu Allāhu ilā ṣūrati ādamiyyin ḥīna qaruba mina al-Nabiyyi (ﷺ) bi-l-waḥy, wa-dhālika qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Fa-awḥā ilā ʿabdihi﴾

Yaʿnī awḥā Allāhu ilā Jibrīl, wa-kāna Jibrīlu (qāba qawsayni aw adnā), qālahu Ibn ʿAbbās wa-l-Ḥasan wa-Qatāda wa-l-Rabīʿ wa-ghayruhum. Wa-ʿan Ibn ʿAbbās ayḍan fī qawlihi taʿālā (thumma dana fa-tadallā) annahu maʿnāhu anna Allāha tabāraka wa-taʿālā (dana) min Muḥammadin (ﷺ) (fa-tadallā). Wa-rawā naḥwahu Anas ibn Mālik ʿan al-Nabiyyi (ﷺ). Wa-l-maʿnā dana minhu amruhu wa-ḥukmuhu. Wa-aṣlu al-tadallī al-nuzūlu ilā al-shayʾi ḥattā yaqruba minhu fa-wuḍiʿa mawḍiʿa al-qurb, qāla Labīd [[Al-bayt fī waṣf faras. Arāda annahu nazala min marbaʾihi wa-huwa ʿalā faraslihi rākib.]]:

Fa-tadallaytu ʿalayhi qāfilan ... wa-ʿalā al-arḍi ghayabātu al-ṭafal

Wa-dhahaba al-Farrāʾu ilā anna al-fāʾa fī (fa-tadallā) bi-maʿnā al-wāw, wa-l-taqdīru thumma tadallā Jibrīlu ʿalayhi l-salāmu wa-dana. Wa-lakinnahu jāʾizun idhā kāna maʿnā al-fiʿlayni wāḥidan aw ka-l-wāḥid qaddamta ayyahumā shiʾta, fa-qulta fa-dana fa-qaruba wa-qaruba fa-dana, wa-shatamanī fa-asāʾa wa-asāʾa fa-shatamanī, li-anna al-shatma wa-l-isāʾa shayʾun wāḥid. Wa-kadhālika qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Iqtaraba al-sāʿatu wa-inshaqqa al-qamar﴾ [[Rājiʿ ṣ. 125 min hādhā l-juzʾ]] al-maʿnā wa-Allāhu aʿlam: inshaqqa al-qamaru wa-iqtarabat al-sāʿah. Wa-qāla al-Jurjānī: fī al-kalāmi taqdīmun wa-taʾkhīr, ayy tadallā fa-dana, li-anna al-tadallī sababu al-dunuww. Wa-qāla Ibn al-Anbārī: thumma tadallā Jibrīlu ayy nazala mina l-samāʾi fa-dana min Muḥammadin (ﷺ). Wa-qāla Ibn ʿAbbās: tadallā al-Rafraf li-Muḥammadin (ﷺ) laylata al-miʿrāj fa-jalasa ʿalayhi thumma rufiʿa fa-dana min rabbihi. Wa-sa-yaʾtī. Wa-man qāla: al-maʿnā fa-istawā Jibrīlu wa-Muḥammadun bi-l-ufuqi l-aʿlā qad yaqūlu: thumma dana Muḥammadun min rabbihi dunuwwa karāmatin fa-tadallā ayy hawā lil-sujūd. Wa-hādhā qawlu l-Ḍaḥḥāk. Qāla al-Qushayrī: wa-qīla ʿalā hādhā tadallā ayy tadallala, ka-qawlika tazannā bi-maʿnā tazannana, wa-hādhā baʿīd, li-anna al-dalālu ghayru marḍiyyin fī ṣifati al-ʿubūdiyya.

Qawluhu taʿālā: ﴿Fa-kāna qāba qawsayni aw adnā﴾ ayy (fa-kāna) Muḥammadun min rabbihi aw min Jibrīla (qāba qawsayni) ayy qadra qawsayni ʿarabiyyatayni. Qālahu Ibn ʿAbbās wa-ʿAṭāʾ wa-l-Farrāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī: fa-in qulta kayfa taqdīru qawlihi: (fa-kāna qāba qawsayni), qultu: taqdīruhu fa-kāna miqdāru masāfati qurbihi mithla qābi qawsayn, fa-ḥudhifat hādhihi al-muḍāfātu kamā qāla Abū ʿAlī fī qawlihi [[Ikhtulifa fī al-qāʾil wa-ṣadr al-bayt:
Fa-adraka ibqāʾa al-ʿarrāda ẓalʿahā
Wa-fī z: (Khuzayma) bi-l-khāʾ al-muʿjama, wa-huwa taḥrīf. Wa-Ḥuzayma (bi-l-muhmala): ism fāris min fursān al-ʿarab. Wa-l-ʿarrādatu: ism faras min khayl al-ʿarab fī al-jāhiliyya.]]:

Wa-qad jaʿalatnī min Ḥuzayma iṣbaʿā, ayy dhā miqdāri masāfati iṣbaʿin. (Aw adnā) ayy ʿalā taqdīrikum, ka-qawlihi taʿālā: (aw yazīdūn) [[Rājiʿ j. 15 ṣ. 130]]. Wa-fī al-Ṣiḥāḥ: wa-taqūlu baynahumā qābu qawsin, wa-qību qawsin wa-qādu qawsin, wa-qīdu qawsin, ayy qadru qawsin. Wa-qaraʾa Zayd ibn ʿAlī (qād) wa-qurīʾa (qīd) wa-(qadr). Dhakarahu al-Zamakhsharī. Wa-l-qābu mā bayna al-maqbaḍi wa-l-siyyati. Wa-li-kulli qawsin qābān. Wa-qāla baʿḍuhum fī qawlihi taʿālā: (qāba qawsayni) arāda qābayi qawsin fa-qalabahu. Wa-fī al-ḥadīth: (wa-la-qābu qawsi aḥadikum mina l-jannati wa-mawḍiʿu qiddihi khayrun mina l-dunyā wa-mā fīhā), wa-l-qiddu al-sawṭ. Wa-fī al-Ṣaḥīḥ ʿan Abī Hurayra qāla: qāla al-Nabiyyu (ﷺ): (wa-la-qābu qawsi aḥadikum mina l-jannati khayrun mina l-dunyā wa-mā fīhā). Wa-innamā ḍuriba al-mathalu bi-l-qaws, li-annahā lā takhtalifu fī l-qāb. Wa-Allāhu aʿlam. Qāla al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ: iʿlam anna mā waqaʿa min iḍāfati al-dunuwwi wa-l-qurbi mina Allāhi aw ilā Allāh falaysa bi-dunuwwi makānin wa-lā qurbi madan, wa-innamā dunuwwu al-Nabiyyi (ﷺ) min rabbihi wa-qurbuhu minhu: ibānatu ʿaẓīmi manzilatihi, wa-tashrīfu rutbatihi, wa-ishrāqu anwāri maʿrifatihi, wa-mushāhadatu asrāri ghaybihi wa-qudratihi. Wa-min Allāhi taʿālā lahu: mabarratun wa-taʾnīsun wa-basṭun wa-ikrām. Wa-yutaʾawwalu fī qawlihi ʿalayhi l-salām: (yanzilu rabbunā ilā samāʾi l-dunyā) ʿalā aḥadi l-wujūh: nuzūlu ijmālin wa-qabūlin wa-iḥsān. Qāla al-Qāḍī: wa-qawluhu: (fa-kāna qāba qawsayni aw adnā) fa-man jaʿala al-ḍamīra ʿāʾidan ilā Allāhi taʿālā lā ilā Jibrīl kāna ʿibāratan ʿan nihāyati al-qurb, wa-luṭfi al-maḥall, wa-īḍāḥi al-maʿrifa, wa-l-ishrāfi ʿalā al-ḥaqīqa min Muḥammadin (ﷺ), wa-ʿibāratan ʿan ijābati al-raghba, wa-qaḍāʾi al-maṭālib, wa-iẓhāri al-taḥaffī, wa-ināfati al-manzila wa-l-qurbi min Allāh, wa-yutaʾawwalu fīhi mā yutaʾawwalu fī qawlihi ʿalayhi l-salām: (man taqarraba minnī shibran taqarrabtu minhu dhirāʿan, wa-man atānī yamshī ataytuhu harwalatan) qurbun bi-l-ijābati wa-l-qabūli, wa-ityānun bi-l-iḥsāni wa-taʿjīlu al-maʾmūl. Wa-qad qīla: (thumma dana) Jibrīlu min rabbihi (fa-kāna qāba qawsayni aw adnā) qālahu Mujāhid. Wa-yadullu ʿalayhi mā rūiya fī l-ḥadīth: (inna aqraba al-malāʾikati mina Allāhi Jibrīlu ʿalayhi l-salām). Wa-qīla: (aw) bi-maʿnā al-wāw ayy qāba qawsayni wa-adnā. Wa-qīla: bi-maʿnā bal ayy bal adnā. Wa-qāla Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab: al-qābu ṣadru al-qawsi al-ʿarabiyya ḥaythu yushaddu ʿalayhi al-sayr alladhī yatanakkabuhu ṣāḥibuhu, wa-li-kulli qawsin qābun wāḥid. Fa-akhbara anna Jibrīla qaruba min Muḥammadin (ﷺ) ka-qurbi qābi qawsayn. Wa-qāla Saʿīd ibn Jubayr wa-ʿAṭāʾ wa-Abū Isḥāq al-Hamdhānī wa-Abū Wāʾil Shaqīq ibn Salama: (fa-kāna qāba qawsayni) ayy qadra dhirāʿayn, wa-l-qawsu al-dhirāʿu yuqāsu bihā kullu shayʾ, wa-hiya lughatu baʿḍi al-Ḥijāziyyīn. Wa-qīla: hiya lughatu Azdi Shanūʾa ayḍan. Wa-qāla al-Kisāʾī: qawluhu: (fa-kāna qāba qawsayni aw adnā) arāda qawsan wāḥidan, ka-qawli al-shāʿir:

Wa-mahmahayni qadhfayni marratayn ... qaṭaʿtuhu bi-l-samti lā bi-l-samtayn [[Al-samtu: al-ṭarīq, wa-maʿnāhu qaṭaʿtuhu ʿalā ṭarīqin wāḥid.]]

Arāda mahmahan wāḥidan. Wa-l-qawsu tudhakkaru wa-tu'annathu, fa-man annatha qāla fī taṣghīrihā quwaysatun, wa-man dhakkara qāla quwaysun, wa-fī al-mathali: huwa min khayri quwaysin sahman. Wa-l-jamʿu qisiyyun wa-qusiyyun wa-aqwāsun wa-qiyās, wa-anshada Abū ʿUbayda:

Wa-watṭara al-asāwira al-qiyāsā [[Qā'iluhu al-Qullākh ibn Ḥazn. Wa-tammatuhu:
Ṣughdiyyatun tanziʿu al-anfāsā
Wa-al-asāwiru: jamʿu uswār wa-huwa al-muqaddamu min asāwirati al-faras. Wa-al-ṣughdu: jīlun min al-ʿajam wa-yuqālu innahu ism balad.
(Māddat qawsa).]]

Surah 53, verses 1–10 (part 3 of 3)

Also, "al-qaws" is the remainder of the leopard in the "jullah," meaning the container. And al-Qaws (the Bow) is a constellation in the sky. As for al-Quws with a damma, it is the monastery (sawma'ah) of the monk. The poet said, mentioning a woman:

"Had you asked me about her and about the man of the two woolen garments in al-Quws..."
[[The verse is by Jarir. Its first half is: "No union, since Hind departed, even if she stood still..."]]

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

This is an exaltation of the revelation that was revealed to him. The meaning of wahy (revelation) has already been mentioned; it is the throwing of a thing swiftly, and from it comes al-wahaa' (haste). The meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, revealed to His servant Muhammad ﷺ what He revealed. It has also been said: the meaning is ﴿He revealed to His servant﴾ [Jibril (peace be upon him)] ﴿what He revealed﴾. [The text between the brackets is missing from manuscripts ح, ز, ل, هـ.] It has also been said: the meaning is that Jibril revealed to the servant of Allah, Muhammad ﷺ, what his Lord had revealed to him. This was said by al-Rabi', al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Qatadah. Qatadah said: Allah revealed to Jibril, and Jibril revealed to Muhammad.

Then it is said: is this revelation undetermined? We do not know it, and we are obligated to believe in it in general terms; or is it known and specified? There are two opinions. Sa'id ibn Jubayr held the second view. He said: Allah revealed to Muhammad: "Did I not find you an orphan and give you shelter? Did I not find you lost and guide you? Did I not find you poor and make you rich?" ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast? And We removed from you your burden, which had weighed down your back? And We raised high your remembrance.﴾ It has also been said: Allah revealed to him that Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, O Muhammad, and forbidden to the nations until your nation enters it.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾

Al-Qurtubi said: Meaning, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie on the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascent). This is because Allah the Exalted placed his sight in his heart, so that he saw his Lord, the Exalted, and Allah made that a vision. It was said: it was a literal vision with the eye. The first view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. In Sahih Muslim, he saw Him with his heart; this is the view of Abu Dharr and a group of the Companions. The second is the view of Anas and a group. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Do you find it strange that intimate friendship (khullah) was for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad (ﷺ)?" Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice." The discussion of this has passed in (al-An'am) [see vol. 7, p. 54] at the words of Allah: ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him, but He perceives the eyes﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b narrated: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart, twice," and then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ A third view: that he saw His majesty and greatness; this was said by al-Hasan. Abu al-'Aliyah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and behind the river I saw a veil, and behind the veil I saw a light; I saw nothing other than that." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "Light; how could I see Him?" The meaning: the light overwhelmed me and dazzled me, and what prevented me from seeing Him was the light. The other narration ("I saw light") supports this. Ibn Mas'ud said: He saw Jibril in his own form twice.

Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria, read "mā kadhdhaba" with the shadda (intensive form), meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not deny what his eye saw that night, but rather confirmed it. So "mā" is its object without any implied preposition, because it is transitive in the intensive form without a particle. It is also possible that "mā" means "alladhi" (that which), with the returning pronoun omitted, and it is also possible that "mā" with the verb forms a verbal noun (masdar). The rest read it unstressed, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what it saw, so the preposition of attribution is dropped. Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped.

That is, "in what you told me." It is also possible that it forms a verbal noun with the verb, and it is possible that it means "alladhi" (that which), i.e., the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what it saw.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta and no alif, meaning "will you deny him?" Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying: "They did not dispute with him; they denied him." One says: "marāhu haqqahu," meaning he denied his right, and "maraytuhu" (I disputed with him). The poet said:

Even if you have forsaken a brother of truthfulness and nobility,
you have indeed disputed with a brother who would never have disputed with you.

That is, you denied him. Al-Mubarrad said: One says "marāhu 'an haqqihi" and "'alā haqqihi" when he prevented him from it and repelled him from it. He said: Like "'alā" in the sense of "'an," is the saying of the Banu Ka'b ibn Rabi'ah: "radiya Allahu 'alayka," meaning "radiya Allahu 'anka" (may Allah be pleased with you). Al-A'raj and Mujahid read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta and no alif, from "amrayta," meaning "will you cause him doubt and make him uncertain?" The rest read "afa-tumārūnahu" with an alif, meaning "will you argue with him and contend with him about whether he saw Allah?" The two meanings overlap, since their disputing is denial. It was said: denial was always from them, and this is a new dispute. They said: "Describe to us the Bayt al-Maqdis, and tell us about our caravan on the road to Syria." As mentioned before [see vol. 10, p. 209].

The Qur'an verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent.﴾ "Nazlatan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), as if he said: "and he certainly saw Him descending in another descent." Ibn 'Abbas said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord again with his heart. Muslim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from him (Ibn 'Abbas), who said: "The heart did not lie about what it saw; and he certainly saw him in another descent." He said: He saw Him with his heart twice. So the words "another descent" refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). If there were ascents and descents many times according to the number of the obligatory prayers, then for every ascent there is a descent. On this basis is the Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) was near the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and in some of those descents. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said, in explaining the words of Allah the Exalted "and he certainly saw him in another descent," that it was Jibril. This is also established in Sahih Muslim. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril at the highest horizon, having six hundred wings, from whose feathers pearls and rubies were scattered." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾. "'Inda" (near) is connected to "ra'ahu" (he saw), as we have explained. The sidr is the jujube tree (nabq), and it is in the sixth heaven, and it is mentioned in the seventh heaven. The hadith on this is in Sahih Muslim. The first is what Murrah narrated from 'Abd Allah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, which is in the sixth heaven, to which whatever ascends from the earth ends and is gathered from it, and to which whatever descends from above it ends and is gathered from it. He said: ﴿when there covered the lote tree what covered it﴾. He said: "Golden locusts." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever among his community did not associate anything with Allah was forgiven the major sins (al-muqhamat). (Al-muqhamat: the grave sins that cast their doers into the Fire, i.e., throw them into it.) The second hadith was narrated by Qatadah from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When I was raised to the lote tree of the utmost boundary in the seventh heaven, its jujubes were like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants. Two apparent rivers flowed from its trunk and two hidden rivers. I said, 'O Jibril, what is this?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of al-Daraqutni. "Nabq" with a kasra on the ba is the fruit of the sidr; its single unit is "nabqah." It is also said "nabq" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the ba; Ya'qub mentioned both in al-Islah, and the latter is the dialect of the Egyptians, though the former is more eloquent and is the one established from the Prophet (ﷺ). al-Tirmidhi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, when the lote tree of the utmost boundary was mentioned to him: "A rider travels in the shade of one of its branches for a hundred years, or a hundred riders take shelter in its shade"; Yahya was in doubt about this; "in it is the golden locust, and its fruit is like jars." Abu 'Isa said: This is a good hadith. I say: The wording of Muslim is similar, from the hadith of Thabit from Anas: "Then I was taken to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants, and its fruit was like jars. When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, it changed, and no one among the creation of Allah can describe its beauty."

There is a difference of opinion on why the lote tree is called "of the utmost boundary," with nine views. First: what has passed from Ibn Mas'ud, that whatever descends from above it ends there, and whatever ascends from below it ends there. Second: that the knowledge of the prophets ends at it, and their knowledge fails beyond it; said by Ibn 'Abbas. Third: that deeds end at it and are gathered from it; said by al-Dahhak. Fourth: because the angels and the prophets end at it and stop there; said by Ka'b. Fifth: it is called the lote tree of the utmost boundary because the souls of the martyrs end at it; said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Sixth: because the souls of the believers end at it [in other copies: "take refuge in it"]; said by Qatadah. Seventh: because everyone who followed the Sunnah and path of Muhammad (ﷺ) ends at it; said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas as well. Eighth: it is a tree on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, to which the knowledge of creation ends; said by Ka'b also. I say: he means, and Allah knows best, that its height and the highest of its branches have passed beyond the heads of the bearers of the Throne; its evidence is what has passed, that its root is in the sixth heaven and its top in the seventh heaven, and then it rose above that until it surpassed the heads of the bearers of the Throne. And Allah knows best. Ninth: it was so named because whoever is raised to it has reached the furthest point of honor. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and it was said to him: "This is the lote tree of the utmost boundary; everyone from your community who follows your Sunnah will end at it." And there it is a tree from whose root flow rivers of water that does not change, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of pure honey. And there it is a tree under whose shade a swift rider travels for a hundred years without crossing it, and one leaf of it covers the whole community. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾. This identifies the location of the Garden of Refuge, that it is near the lote tree of the utmost boundary. 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Abu Sabrah al-Juhani, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid read "'indahā jannatu al-mab-it" (the Garden of the Night's Lodging). Mujahid said: He means "ajannahu" (it covered him), and the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Akhfash said: "adrakahu" (it overtook him), as you say "jannahu al-layl" (the night covered him), meaning it concealed him and overtook him. The common reading is "jannatu al-ma'wa." Al-Hasan said: It is the one to which the God-fearing will go. It was said: it is the Garden to which the souls of the martyrs go; said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is to the right of the Throne. It was said: it is the Garden to which Adam, peace be upon him, took refuge until he was removed from it, and it is in the seventh heaven [in other copies: "the fourth," and so it is in the margin of al-Jamal from al-Qurtubi]. It was said: the souls of all believers are in the Garden of Refuge. It is called the Garden of Refuge only because the souls of the believers take refuge in it, and it is beneath the Throne, so they enjoy its bliss and breathe in its pleasant fragrance. It was said: because Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, take refuge in it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 11–18 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ibn Mas'ud and his companions said: it was a moth of gold. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas narrated it as a marfu' report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). It has already been mentioned in Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, as his statement. al-Hasan said: the light of the Lord of the worlds covered it, and so it was illuminated. al-Qushayri said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "What covered it?" He said: "A moth of gold." In another report: "A light from Allah covered it, so that no one could look at it." al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the light of the Lord covered it, and the angels settled on it as crows settle on a tree. And from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "I saw the lote-tree covered by a moth of gold, and I saw upon every leaf an angel standing, glorifying [Allah, exalted is He]" [[Omitted from z, l, h.]]. This is His saying: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. It was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi [[After this, the following text is quoted from al-Qurtubi in his tafsir: It was said: angels cover it, as if they were birds ascending to it, longing, seeking blessing, visiting, as people visit the Ka'bah. In the hadith of the Ascension, it is related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibril took me to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, whose leaves were like the ears of elephants, and whose fruit was like the jars of Hajar." He said: "When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah, it changed, so that no one among the creation of Allah was able to describe its beauty. Then He revealed to me what He revealed, and made obligatory upon me fifty prayers each day and night." It was also said: the lights of Allah cover it, because when the Prophet (ﷺ) reached it, his Lord manifested Himself to it as He manifested Himself to the mountain, and the lights appeared. But the lote-tree was stronger and more firm than the mountain, so the mountain was made into dust, while the tree did not move, and Musa fell down unconscious, while Muhammad (ﷺ) did not tremble. It was also said: He left it unspecified out of glorification of it. And "covering" means "concealing".]]. Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾ — it was a locust of gold, and he related it as marfu'. Mujahid said: it is a green rafraf. And from him (peace be upon him): "It is covered by a rafraf of green birds." And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is covered by the Lord of Might, meaning His command, as in Sahih Muslim, marfu': "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it." It was also said: this is the magnification of the matter, as if He said: when there covered the lote-tree what Allah made known of the signs of His dominion. And likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

(﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down; so there covered them what covered﴾) and similar to it: (﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾) [[See vol. 18, p. 256]]. al-Mawardi said in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was the lote-tree chosen for this matter over other trees? It is answered: because the lote-tree is distinguished by three attributes: extensive shade, a delicious taste, and a fragrant scent. It resembles faith, which combines speech, action and intention. Its shade is for faith like action, because it extends beyond; its taste is like intention, because it is hidden within; and its scent is like speech, because it is manifest.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, saying: Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from 'Abd Allah ibn Habashi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever cuts a lote-tree, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire." Abu Dawud was asked about the meaning of this hadith, and he said: this hadith is abridged; it means: whoever cuts a lote-tree in a desert, under which the wayfarer and the animals seek shade, wantonly and unjustly, without a right he has in it, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it did not turn to the right or the left, nor exceed the limit of what he saw. It was said: he did not go beyond what he was commanded. It was said: he did not extend his sight to anything other than what he saw of the signs. This is a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) good manners [[In b, z, h, s, l, and h: (good manners of the Prophet).]] in that station, for he did not turn right or left.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. al-Bayhaqi mentioned from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a green rafraf that filled the horizon of the sky. And from him he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a green garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. al-Bayhaqi said: his saying in the hadith "he saw a rafraf" means Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form, upon a rafraf, and the rafraf is a carpet; it is also said: a cushion. It is also said: rather, it is a garment which he wore. It is related that he saw him in a garment of rafraf. I say: al-Tirmidhi narrated it from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ — he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih. I say: it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ that it is by inversion of order, meaning: the rafraf descended to Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Ascension, and he sat upon it, then it was raised and he drew near to his Lord. He said: "Jibril left me, the voices ceased from me, and I heard the speech of my Lord." According to this, the rafraf is that upon which one sits, like a carpet and the like; and in the first sense it is Jibril. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form in which he appears in the heavens. Likewise in Sahih Muslim from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — he said: he saw Jibril in his form, having six hundred wings. It is not far from this that he was in a garment of rafraf and upon a rafraf. And Allah knows best. al-Dahhak said: he saw the lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. From Ibn Mas'ud: he saw what covered the lote-tree of the moths of gold; related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: he saw the Ascension. It was also said: it is what he saw that night on his journey, in his return and his beginning, and this is the best view. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 204]]. The word "min" (of) may be partitive, and "al-Kubra" (the greatest) is the object of "ra'a" (saw), and it is in origin an attribute of "ayat" (signs), but it is made feminine singular to agree with the heads of the signs. Also, it is permissible to describe a plural noun with a feminine adjective, as in His saying: ﴿And for him therein are other uses﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 187]]. It was also said: "al-Kubra" is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest. It is permissible that "min" is superfluous, meaning: he saw the greatest signs of his Lord. It was also said: there is inversion, meaning: he saw the greatest of the signs of his Lord.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾

Al-Qurtubi said: Meaning, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie on the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascent). This is because Allah the Exalted placed his sight in his heart, so that he saw his Lord, the Exalted, and Allah made that a vision. It was said: it was a literal vision with the eye. The first view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. In Sahih Muslim, he saw Him with his heart; this is the view of Abu Dharr and a group of the Companions. The second is the view of Anas and a group. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Do you find it strange that intimate friendship (khullah) was for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad (ﷺ)?" Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice." The discussion of this has passed in (al-An'am) [see vol. 7, p. 54] at the words of Allah: ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him, but He perceives the eyes﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b narrated: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart, twice," and then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ A third view: that he saw His majesty and greatness; this was said by al-Hasan. Abu al-'Aliyah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and behind the river I saw a veil, and behind the veil I saw a light; I saw nothing other than that." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "Light; how could I see Him?" The meaning: the light overwhelmed me and dazzled me, and what prevented me from seeing Him was the light. The other narration ("I saw light") supports this. Ibn Mas'ud said: He saw Jibril in his own form twice.

Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria, read "mā kadhdhaba" with the shadda (intensive form), meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not deny what his eye saw that night, but rather confirmed it. So "mā" is its object without any implied preposition, because it is transitive in the intensive form without a particle. It is also possible that "mā" means "alladhi" (that which), with the returning pronoun omitted, and it is also possible that "mā" with the verb forms a verbal noun (masdar). The rest read it unstressed, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what it saw, so the preposition of attribution is dropped. Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped.

That is, "in what you told me." It is also possible that it forms a verbal noun with the verb, and it is possible that it means "alladhi" (that which), i.e., the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what it saw.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta and no alif, meaning "will you deny him?" Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying: "They did not dispute with him; they denied him." One says: "marāhu haqqahu," meaning he denied his right, and "maraytuhu" (I disputed with him). The poet said:

Even if you have forsaken a brother of truthfulness and nobility,
you have indeed disputed with a brother who would never have disputed with you.

That is, you denied him. Al-Mubarrad said: One says "marāhu 'an haqqihi" and "'alā haqqihi" when he prevented him from it and repelled him from it. He said: Like "'alā" in the sense of "'an," is the saying of the Banu Ka'b ibn Rabi'ah: "radiya Allahu 'alayka," meaning "radiya Allahu 'anka" (may Allah be pleased with you). Al-A'raj and Mujahid read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta and no alif, from "amrayta," meaning "will you cause him doubt and make him uncertain?" The rest read "afa-tumārūnahu" with an alif, meaning "will you argue with him and contend with him about whether he saw Allah?" The two meanings overlap, since their disputing is denial. It was said: denial was always from them, and this is a new dispute. They said: "Describe to us the Bayt al-Maqdis, and tell us about our caravan on the road to Syria." As mentioned before [see vol. 10, p. 209].

The Qur'an verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent.﴾ "Nazlatan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), as if he said: "and he certainly saw Him descending in another descent." Ibn 'Abbas said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord again with his heart. Muslim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from him (Ibn 'Abbas), who said: "The heart did not lie about what it saw; and he certainly saw him in another descent." He said: He saw Him with his heart twice. So the words "another descent" refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). If there were ascents and descents many times according to the number of the obligatory prayers, then for every ascent there is a descent. On this basis is the Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) was near the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and in some of those descents. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said, in explaining the words of Allah the Exalted "and he certainly saw him in another descent," that it was Jibril. This is also established in Sahih Muslim. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril at the highest horizon, having six hundred wings, from whose feathers pearls and rubies were scattered." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾. "'Inda" (near) is connected to "ra'ahu" (he saw), as we have explained. The sidr is the jujube tree (nabq), and it is in the sixth heaven, and it is mentioned in the seventh heaven. The hadith on this is in Sahih Muslim. The first is what Murrah narrated from 'Abd Allah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, which is in the sixth heaven, to which whatever ascends from the earth ends and is gathered from it, and to which whatever descends from above it ends and is gathered from it. He said: ﴿when there covered the lote tree what covered it﴾. He said: "Golden locusts." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever among his community did not associate anything with Allah was forgiven the major sins (al-muqhamat). (Al-muqhamat: the grave sins that cast their doers into the Fire, i.e., throw them into it.) The second hadith was narrated by Qatadah from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When I was raised to the lote tree of the utmost boundary in the seventh heaven, its jujubes were like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants. Two apparent rivers flowed from its trunk and two hidden rivers. I said, 'O Jibril, what is this?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of al-Daraqutni. "Nabq" with a kasra on the ba is the fruit of the sidr; its single unit is "nabqah." It is also said "nabq" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the ba; Ya'qub mentioned both in al-Islah, and the latter is the dialect of the Egyptians, though the former is more eloquent and is the one established from the Prophet (ﷺ). al-Tirmidhi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, when the lote tree of the utmost boundary was mentioned to him: "A rider travels in the shade of one of its branches for a hundred years, or a hundred riders take shelter in its shade"; Yahya was in doubt about this; "in it is the golden locust, and its fruit is like jars." Abu 'Isa said: This is a good hadith. I say: The wording of Muslim is similar, from the hadith of Thabit from Anas: "Then I was taken to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants, and its fruit was like jars. When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, it changed, and no one among the creation of Allah can describe its beauty."

There is a difference of opinion on why the lote tree is called "of the utmost boundary," with nine views. First: what has passed from Ibn Mas'ud, that whatever descends from above it ends there, and whatever ascends from below it ends there. Second: that the knowledge of the prophets ends at it, and their knowledge fails beyond it; said by Ibn 'Abbas. Third: that deeds end at it and are gathered from it; said by al-Dahhak. Fourth: because the angels and the prophets end at it and stop there; said by Ka'b. Fifth: it is called the lote tree of the utmost boundary because the souls of the martyrs end at it; said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Sixth: because the souls of the believers end at it [in other copies: "take refuge in it"]; said by Qatadah. Seventh: because everyone who followed the Sunnah and path of Muhammad (ﷺ) ends at it; said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas as well. Eighth: it is a tree on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, to which the knowledge of creation ends; said by Ka'b also. I say: he means, and Allah knows best, that its height and the highest of its branches have passed beyond the heads of the bearers of the Throne; its evidence is what has passed, that its root is in the sixth heaven and its top in the seventh heaven, and then it rose above that until it surpassed the heads of the bearers of the Throne. And Allah knows best. Ninth: it was so named because whoever is raised to it has reached the furthest point of honor. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and it was said to him: "This is the lote tree of the utmost boundary; everyone from your community who follows your Sunnah will end at it." And there it is a tree from whose root flow rivers of water that does not change, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of pure honey. And there it is a tree under whose shade a swift rider travels for a hundred years without crossing it, and one leaf of it covers the whole community. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾. This identifies the location of the Garden of Refuge, that it is near the lote tree of the utmost boundary. 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Abu Sabrah al-Juhani, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid read "'indahā jannatu al-mab-it" (the Garden of the Night's Lodging). Mujahid said: He means "ajannahu" (it covered him), and the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Akhfash said: "adrakahu" (it overtook him), as you say "jannahu al-layl" (the night covered him), meaning it concealed him and overtook him. The common reading is "jannatu al-ma'wa." Al-Hasan said: It is the one to which the God-fearing will go. It was said: it is the Garden to which the souls of the martyrs go; said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is to the right of the Throne. It was said: it is the Garden to which Adam, peace be upon him, took refuge until he was removed from it, and it is in the seventh heaven [in other copies: "the fourth," and so it is in the margin of al-Jamal from al-Qurtubi]. It was said: the souls of all believers are in the Garden of Refuge. It is called the Garden of Refuge only because the souls of the believers take refuge in it, and it is beneath the Throne, so they enjoy its bliss and breathe in its pleasant fragrance. It was said: because Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, take refuge in it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 11–18 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ibn Mas'ud and his companions said: it was a moth of gold. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas narrated it as a marfu' report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). It has already been mentioned in Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, as his statement. al-Hasan said: the light of the Lord of the worlds covered it, and so it was illuminated. al-Qushayri said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "What covered it?" He said: "A moth of gold." In another report: "A light from Allah covered it, so that no one could look at it." al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the light of the Lord covered it, and the angels settled on it as crows settle on a tree. And from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "I saw the lote-tree covered by a moth of gold, and I saw upon every leaf an angel standing, glorifying [Allah, exalted is He]" [[Omitted from z, l, h.]]. This is His saying: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. It was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi [[After this, the following text is quoted from al-Qurtubi in his tafsir: It was said: angels cover it, as if they were birds ascending to it, longing, seeking blessing, visiting, as people visit the Ka'bah. In the hadith of the Ascension, it is related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibril took me to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, whose leaves were like the ears of elephants, and whose fruit was like the jars of Hajar." He said: "When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah, it changed, so that no one among the creation of Allah was able to describe its beauty. Then He revealed to me what He revealed, and made obligatory upon me fifty prayers each day and night." It was also said: the lights of Allah cover it, because when the Prophet (ﷺ) reached it, his Lord manifested Himself to it as He manifested Himself to the mountain, and the lights appeared. But the lote-tree was stronger and more firm than the mountain, so the mountain was made into dust, while the tree did not move, and Musa fell down unconscious, while Muhammad (ﷺ) did not tremble. It was also said: He left it unspecified out of glorification of it. And "covering" means "concealing".]]. Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾ — it was a locust of gold, and he related it as marfu'. Mujahid said: it is a green rafraf. And from him (peace be upon him): "It is covered by a rafraf of green birds." And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is covered by the Lord of Might, meaning His command, as in Sahih Muslim, marfu': "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it." It was also said: this is the magnification of the matter, as if He said: when there covered the lote-tree what Allah made known of the signs of His dominion. And likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

(﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down; so there covered them what covered﴾) and similar to it: (﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾) [[See vol. 18, p. 256]]. al-Mawardi said in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was the lote-tree chosen for this matter over other trees? It is answered: because the lote-tree is distinguished by three attributes: extensive shade, a delicious taste, and a fragrant scent. It resembles faith, which combines speech, action and intention. Its shade is for faith like action, because it extends beyond; its taste is like intention, because it is hidden within; and its scent is like speech, because it is manifest.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, saying: Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from 'Abd Allah ibn Habashi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever cuts a lote-tree, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire." Abu Dawud was asked about the meaning of this hadith, and he said: this hadith is abridged; it means: whoever cuts a lote-tree in a desert, under which the wayfarer and the animals seek shade, wantonly and unjustly, without a right he has in it, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it did not turn to the right or the left, nor exceed the limit of what he saw. It was said: he did not go beyond what he was commanded. It was said: he did not extend his sight to anything other than what he saw of the signs. This is a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) good manners [[In b, z, h, s, l, and h: (good manners of the Prophet).]] in that station, for he did not turn right or left.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. al-Bayhaqi mentioned from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a green rafraf that filled the horizon of the sky. And from him he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a green garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. al-Bayhaqi said: his saying in the hadith "he saw a rafraf" means Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form, upon a rafraf, and the rafraf is a carpet; it is also said: a cushion. It is also said: rather, it is a garment which he wore. It is related that he saw him in a garment of rafraf. I say: al-Tirmidhi narrated it from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ — he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih. I say: it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ that it is by inversion of order, meaning: the rafraf descended to Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Ascension, and he sat upon it, then it was raised and he drew near to his Lord. He said: "Jibril left me, the voices ceased from me, and I heard the speech of my Lord." According to this, the rafraf is that upon which one sits, like a carpet and the like; and in the first sense it is Jibril. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form in which he appears in the heavens. Likewise in Sahih Muslim from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — he said: he saw Jibril in his form, having six hundred wings. It is not far from this that he was in a garment of rafraf and upon a rafraf. And Allah knows best. al-Dahhak said: he saw the lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. From Ibn Mas'ud: he saw what covered the lote-tree of the moths of gold; related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: he saw the Ascension. It was also said: it is what he saw that night on his journey, in his return and his beginning, and this is the best view. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 204]]. The word "min" (of) may be partitive, and "al-Kubra" (the greatest) is the object of "ra'a" (saw), and it is in origin an attribute of "ayat" (signs), but it is made feminine singular to agree with the heads of the signs. Also, it is permissible to describe a plural noun with a feminine adjective, as in His saying: ﴿And for him therein are other uses﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 187]]. It was also said: "al-Kubra" is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest. It is permissible that "min" is superfluous, meaning: he saw the greatest signs of his Lord. It was also said: there is inversion, meaning: he saw the greatest of the signs of his Lord.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾

Al-Qurtubi said: Meaning, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie on the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascent). This is because Allah the Exalted placed his sight in his heart, so that he saw his Lord, the Exalted, and Allah made that a vision. It was said: it was a literal vision with the eye. The first view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. In Sahih Muslim, he saw Him with his heart; this is the view of Abu Dharr and a group of the Companions. The second is the view of Anas and a group. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Do you find it strange that intimate friendship (khullah) was for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad (ﷺ)?" Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice." The discussion of this has passed in (al-An'am) [see vol. 7, p. 54] at the words of Allah: ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him, but He perceives the eyes﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b narrated: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart, twice," and then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ A third view: that he saw His majesty and greatness; this was said by al-Hasan. Abu al-'Aliyah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and behind the river I saw a veil, and behind the veil I saw a light; I saw nothing other than that." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "Light; how could I see Him?" The meaning: the light overwhelmed me and dazzled me, and what prevented me from seeing Him was the light. The other narration ("I saw light") supports this. Ibn Mas'ud said: He saw Jibril in his own form twice.

The rest read it unstressed, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what it saw, so the preposition of attribution is dropped. Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped.

That is, "in what you told me." It is also possible that it forms a verbal noun with the verb, and it is possible that it means "alladhi" (that which), i.e., the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what it saw.

It was said: denial was always from them, and this is a new dispute. They said: "Describe to us the Bayt al-Maqdis, and tell us about our caravan on the road to Syria." As mentioned before [see vol. 10, p. 209].

Ibn 'Abbas said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord again with his heart. So the words "another descent" refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). If there were ascents and descents many times according to the number of the obligatory prayers, then for every ascent there is a descent. On this basis is the Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) was near the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and in some of those descents.
