Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾ — it was a locust of gold, and he related it as marfu'. Mujahid said: it is a green rafraf. And from him (peace be upon him): "It is covered by a rafraf of green birds." And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is covered by the Lord of Might, meaning His command, as in Sahih Muslim, marfu': "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it." It was also said: this is the magnification of the matter, as if He said: when there covered the lote-tree what Allah made known of the signs of His dominion. And likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

(﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down; so there covered them what covered﴾) and similar to it: (﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾) [[See vol. 18, p. 256]]. al-Mawardi said in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was the lote-tree chosen for this matter over other trees? It is answered: because the lote-tree is distinguished by three attributes: extensive shade, a delicious taste, and a fragrant scent. It resembles faith, which combines speech, action and intention. Its shade is for faith like action, because it extends beyond; its taste is like intention, because it is hidden within; and its scent is like speech, because it is manifest.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, saying: Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from 'Abd Allah ibn Habashi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever cuts a lote-tree, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire." Abu Dawud was asked about the meaning of this hadith, and he said: this hadith is abridged; it means: whoever cuts a lote-tree in a desert, under which the wayfarer and the animals seek shade, wantonly and unjustly, without a right he has in it, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it did not turn to the right or the left, nor exceed the limit of what he saw. It was said: he did not go beyond what he was commanded. It was said: he did not extend his sight to anything other than what he saw of the signs. This is a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) good manners [[In b, z, h, s, l, and h: (good manners of the Prophet).]] in that station, for he did not turn right or left.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. al-Bayhaqi mentioned from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a green rafraf that filled the horizon of the sky. And from him he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a green garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. al-Bayhaqi said: his saying in the hadith "he saw a rafraf" means Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form, upon a rafraf, and the rafraf is a carpet; it is also said: a cushion. It is also said: rather, it is a garment which he wore. It is related that he saw him in a garment of rafraf. I say: al-Tirmidhi narrated it from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ — he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih. I say: it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ that it is by inversion of order, meaning: the rafraf descended to Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Ascension, and he sat upon it, then it was raised and he drew near to his Lord. He said: "Jibril left me, the voices ceased from me, and I heard the speech of my Lord." According to this, the rafraf is that upon which one sits, like a carpet and the like; and in the first sense it is Jibril. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form in which he appears in the heavens. Likewise in Sahih Muslim from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — he said: he saw Jibril in his form, having six hundred wings. It is not far from this that he was in a garment of rafraf and upon a rafraf. And Allah knows best. al-Dahhak said: he saw the lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. From Ibn Mas'ud: he saw what covered the lote-tree of the moths of gold; related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: he saw the Ascension. It was also said: it is what he saw that night on his journey, in his return and his beginning, and this is the best view. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 204]]. The word "min" (of) may be partitive, and "al-Kubra" (the greatest) is the object of "ra'a" (saw), and it is in origin an attribute of "ayat" (signs), but it is made feminine singular to agree with the heads of the signs. Also, it is permissible to describe a plural noun with a feminine adjective, as in His saying: ﴿And for him therein are other uses﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 187]]. It was also said: "al-Kubra" is an attribute of an omitted noun, meaning: he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest. It is permissible that "min" is superfluous, meaning: he saw the greatest signs of his Lord. It was also said: there is inversion, meaning: he saw the greatest of the signs of his Lord.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾

Al-Qurtubi said: Meaning, the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie on the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Ascent). This is because Allah the Exalted placed his sight in his heart, so that he saw his Lord, the Exalted, and Allah made that a vision. It was said: it was a literal vision with the eye. The first view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. In Sahih Muslim, he saw Him with his heart; this is the view of Abu Dharr and a group of the Companions. The second is the view of Anas and a group. Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Do you find it strange that intimate friendship (khullah) was for Ibrahim, speech for Musa, and vision for Muhammad (ﷺ)?" Also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "As for us, the Banu Hashim, we say that Muhammad saw his Lord twice." The discussion of this has passed in (al-An'am) [see vol. 7, p. 54] at the words of Allah: ﴿Eyes do not perceive Him, but He perceives the eyes﴾. Muhammad ibn Ka'b narrated: We said, "O Messenger of Allah, did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw Him with my heart, twice," and then he recited: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw.﴾ A third view: that he saw His majesty and greatness; this was said by al-Hasan. Abu al-'Aliyah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "I saw a river, and behind the river I saw a veil, and behind the veil I saw a light; I saw nothing other than that." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Dharr, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "Light; how could I see Him?" The meaning: the light overwhelmed me and dazzled me, and what prevented me from seeing Him was the light. The other narration ("I saw light") supports this. Ibn Mas'ud said: He saw Jibril in his own form twice.

Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir and the people of Syria, read "mā kadhdhaba" with the shadda (intensive form), meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not deny what his eye saw that night, but rather confirmed it. So "mā" is its object without any implied preposition, because it is transitive in the intensive form without a particle. It is also possible that "mā" means "alladhi" (that which), with the returning pronoun omitted, and it is also possible that "mā" with the verb forms a verbal noun (masdar). The rest read it unstressed, meaning: the heart of Muhammad did not lie about what it saw, so the preposition of attribution is dropped. Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

If you had been truthful in what you told me,
you would have escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped.

That is, "in what you told me." It is also possible that it forms a verbal noun with the verb, and it is possible that it means "alladhi" (that which), i.e., the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not lie about what it saw.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "afa-tamrūnahu" with a fatha on the ta and no alif, meaning "will you deny him?" Abu 'Ubayd preferred this, saying: "They did not dispute with him; they denied him." One says: "marāhu haqqahu," meaning he denied his right, and "maraytuhu" (I disputed with him). The poet said:

Even if you have forsaken a brother of truthfulness and nobility,
you have indeed disputed with a brother who would never have disputed with you.

That is, you denied him. Al-Mubarrad said: One says "marāhu 'an haqqihi" and "'alā haqqihi" when he prevented him from it and repelled him from it. He said: Like "'alā" in the sense of "'an," is the saying of the Banu Ka'b ibn Rabi'ah: "radiya Allahu 'alayka," meaning "radiya Allahu 'anka" (may Allah be pleased with you). Al-A'raj and Mujahid read "afa-tumrūnahu" with a damma on the ta and no alif, from "amrayta," meaning "will you cause him doubt and make him uncertain?" The rest read "afa-tumārūnahu" with an alif, meaning "will you argue with him and contend with him about whether he saw Allah?" The two meanings overlap, since their disputing is denial. It was said: denial was always from them, and this is a new dispute. They said: "Describe to us the Bayt al-Maqdis, and tell us about our caravan on the road to Syria." As mentioned before [see vol. 10, p. 209].

The Qur'an verse: ﴿And he certainly saw him in another descent.﴾ "Nazlatan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), as if he said: "and he certainly saw Him descending in another descent." Ibn 'Abbas said: Muhammad (ﷺ) saw his Lord again with his heart. Muslim narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, from him (Ibn 'Abbas), who said: "The heart did not lie about what it saw; and he certainly saw him in another descent." He said: He saw Him with his heart twice. So the words "another descent" refer to Muhammad (ﷺ). If there were ascents and descents many times according to the number of the obligatory prayers, then for every ascent there is a descent. On this basis is the Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) was near the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and in some of those descents. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah said, in explaining the words of Allah the Exalted "and he certainly saw him in another descent," that it was Jibril. This is also established in Sahih Muslim. Ibn Mas'ud said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I saw Jibril at the highest horizon, having six hundred wings, from whose feathers pearls and rubies were scattered." This was mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near the lote tree of the utmost boundary﴾. "'Inda" (near) is connected to "ra'ahu" (he saw), as we have explained. The sidr is the jujube tree (nabq), and it is in the sixth heaven, and it is mentioned in the seventh heaven. The hadith on this is in Sahih Muslim. The first is what Murrah narrated from 'Abd Allah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, which is in the sixth heaven, to which whatever ascends from the earth ends and is gathered from it, and to which whatever descends from above it ends and is gathered from it. He said: ﴿when there covered the lote tree what covered it﴾. He said: "Golden locusts." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given three things: he was given the five prayers, he was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever among his community did not associate anything with Allah was forgiven the major sins (al-muqhamat). (Al-muqhamat: the grave sins that cast their doers into the Fire, i.e., throw them into it.) The second hadith was narrated by Qatadah from Anas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When I was raised to the lote tree of the utmost boundary in the seventh heaven, its jujubes were like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants. Two apparent rivers flowed from its trunk and two hidden rivers. I said, 'O Jibril, what is this?' He said: 'As for the two hidden ones, they are in Paradise; as for the two apparent ones, they are the Nile and the Euphrates.'" This is the wording of al-Daraqutni. "Nabq" with a kasra on the ba is the fruit of the sidr; its single unit is "nabqah." It is also said "nabq" with a fatha on the nun and a sukun on the ba; Ya'qub mentioned both in al-Islah, and the latter is the dialect of the Egyptians, though the former is more eloquent and is the one established from the Prophet (ﷺ). al-Tirmidhi narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say, when the lote tree of the utmost boundary was mentioned to him: "A rider travels in the shade of one of its branches for a hundred years, or a hundred riders take shelter in its shade"; Yahya was in doubt about this; "in it is the golden locust, and its fruit is like jars." Abu 'Isa said: This is a good hadith. I say: The wording of Muslim is similar, from the hadith of Thabit from Anas: "Then I was taken to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and its leaves were like the ears of elephants, and its fruit was like jars. When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, it changed, and no one among the creation of Allah can describe its beauty."

There is a difference of opinion on why the lote tree is called "of the utmost boundary," with nine views. First: what has passed from Ibn Mas'ud, that whatever descends from above it ends there, and whatever ascends from below it ends there. Second: that the knowledge of the prophets ends at it, and their knowledge fails beyond it; said by Ibn 'Abbas. Third: that deeds end at it and are gathered from it; said by al-Dahhak. Fourth: because the angels and the prophets end at it and stop there; said by Ka'b. Fifth: it is called the lote tree of the utmost boundary because the souls of the martyrs end at it; said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Sixth: because the souls of the believers end at it [in other copies: "take refuge in it"]; said by Qatadah. Seventh: because everyone who followed the Sunnah and path of Muhammad (ﷺ) ends at it; said by 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas as well. Eighth: it is a tree on the heads of the bearers of the Throne, to which the knowledge of creation ends; said by Ka'b also. I say: he means, and Allah knows best, that its height and the highest of its branches have passed beyond the heads of the bearers of the Throne; its evidence is what has passed, that its root is in the sixth heaven and its top in the seventh heaven, and then it rose above that until it surpassed the heads of the bearers of the Throne. And Allah knows best. Ninth: it was so named because whoever is raised to it has reached the furthest point of honor. It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the Night Journey, he was brought to the lote tree of the utmost boundary, and it was said to him: "This is the lote tree of the utmost boundary; everyone from your community who follows your Sunnah will end at it." And there it is a tree from whose root flow rivers of water that does not change, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to the drinkers, and rivers of pure honey. And there it is a tree under whose shade a swift rider travels for a hundred years without crossing it, and one leaf of it covers the whole community. This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿near it is the Garden of Refuge﴾. This identifies the location of the Garden of Refuge, that it is near the lote tree of the utmost boundary. 'Ali, Abu Hurayrah, Anas, Abu Sabrah al-Juhani, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and Mujahid read "'indahā jannatu al-mab-it" (the Garden of the Night's Lodging). Mujahid said: He means "ajannahu" (it covered him), and the pronoun refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Akhfash said: "adrakahu" (it overtook him), as you say "jannahu al-layl" (the night covered him), meaning it concealed him and overtook him. The common reading is "jannatu al-ma'wa." Al-Hasan said: It is the one to which the God-fearing will go. It was said: it is the Garden to which the souls of the martyrs go; said by Ibn 'Abbas, and it is to the right of the Throne. It was said: it is the Garden to which Adam, peace be upon him, took refuge until he was removed from it, and it is in the seventh heaven [in other copies: "the fourth," and so it is in the margin of al-Jamal from al-Qurtubi]. It was said: the souls of all believers are in the Garden of Refuge. It is called the Garden of Refuge only because the souls of the believers take refuge in it, and it is beneath the Throne, so they enjoy its bliss and breathe in its pleasant fragrance. It was said: because Jibril and Mika'il, peace be upon them both, take refuge in it. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 11–18 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Ibn Mas'ud and his companions said: it was a moth of gold. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas narrated it as a marfu' report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). It has already been mentioned in Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, as his statement. al-Hasan said: the light of the Lord of the worlds covered it, and so it was illuminated. al-Qushayri said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, "What covered it?" He said: "A moth of gold." In another report: "A light from Allah covered it, so that no one could look at it." al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the light of the Lord covered it, and the angels settled on it as crows settle on a tree. And from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "I saw the lote-tree covered by a moth of gold, and I saw upon every leaf an angel standing, glorifying [Allah, exalted is He]" [[Omitted from z, l, h.]]. This is His saying: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾. It was mentioned by al-Mahdawi and al-Tha'labi [[After this, the following text is quoted from al-Qurtubi in his tafsir: It was said: angels cover it, as if they were birds ascending to it, longing, seeking blessing, visiting, as people visit the Ka'bah. In the hadith of the Ascension, it is related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibril took me to the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, whose leaves were like the ears of elephants, and whose fruit was like the jars of Hajar." He said: "When there covered it what covered it by the command of Allah, it changed, so that no one among the creation of Allah was able to describe its beauty. Then He revealed to me what He revealed, and made obligatory upon me fifty prayers each day and night." It was also said: the lights of Allah cover it, because when the Prophet (ﷺ) reached it, his Lord manifested Himself to it as He manifested Himself to the mountain, and the lights appeared. But the lote-tree was stronger and more firm than the mountain, so the mountain was made into dust, while the tree did not move, and Musa fell down unconscious, while Muhammad (ﷺ) did not tremble. It was also said: He left it unspecified out of glorification of it. And "covering" means "concealing".]]. Anas ibn Malik said: ﴿When that which covers the lote-tree covered it﴾ — it was a locust of gold, and he related it as marfu'. Mujahid said: it is a green rafraf. And from him (peace be upon him): "It is covered by a rafraf of green birds." And from Ibn 'Abbas: it is covered by the Lord of Might, meaning His command, as in Sahih Muslim, marfu': "When there covered it of the command of Allah what covered it." It was also said: this is the magnification of the matter, as if He said: when there covered the lote-tree what Allah made known of the signs of His dominion. And likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾.

(﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down; so there covered them what covered﴾) and similar to it: (﴿The Inevitable Reality, what is the Inevitable Reality?﴾) [[See vol. 18, p. 256]]. al-Mawardi said in his Ma'ani al-Qur'an: If it is asked, why was the lote-tree chosen for this matter over other trees? It is answered: because the lote-tree is distinguished by three attributes: extensive shade, a delicious taste, and a fragrant scent. It resembles faith, which combines speech, action and intention. Its shade is for faith like action, because it extends beyond; its taste is like intention, because it is hidden within; and its scent is like speech, because it is manifest.

Abu Dawud related in his Sunan, saying: Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: Abu Usamah narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Uthman ibn Abi Sulayman, from Sa'id ibn Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from 'Abd Allah ibn Habashi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever cuts a lote-tree, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire." Abu Dawud was asked about the meaning of this hadith, and he said: this hadith is abridged; it means: whoever cuts a lote-tree in a desert, under which the wayfarer and the animals seek shade, wantonly and unjustly, without a right he has in it, Allah will thrust his head into the Fire.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, it did not turn to the right or the left, nor exceed the limit of what he saw. It was said: he did not go beyond what he was commanded. It was said: he did not extend his sight to anything other than what he saw of the signs. This is a description of the Prophet's (ﷺ) good manners [[In b, z, h, s, l, and h: (good manners of the Prophet).]] in that station, for he did not turn right or left.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a rafraf that filled the horizon. al-Bayhaqi mentioned from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — Ibn 'Abbas said: he saw a green rafraf that filled the horizon of the sky. And from him he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a green garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. al-Bayhaqi said: his saying in the hadith "he saw a rafraf" means Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form, upon a rafraf, and the rafraf is a carpet; it is also said: a cushion. It is also said: rather, it is a garment which he wore. It is related that he saw him in a garment of rafraf. I say: al-Tirmidhi narrated it from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ — he said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in a garment of rafraf, which filled what is between the heaven and the earth. He said: this is a hadith hasan sahih. I say: it has been related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then he drew near and came down﴾ that it is by inversion of order, meaning: the rafraf descended to Muhammad (ﷺ) on the night of the Ascension, and he sat upon it, then it was raised and he drew near to his Lord. He said: "Jibril left me, the voices ceased from me, and I heard the speech of my Lord." According to this, the rafraf is that upon which one sits, like a carpet and the like; and in the first sense it is Jibril. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: he saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form in which he appears in the heavens. Likewise in Sahih Muslim from 'Abd Allah, who said: ﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ — he said: he saw Jibril in his form, having six hundred wings. It is not far from this that he was in a garment of rafraf and upon a rafraf. And Allah knows best. al-Dahhak said: he saw the lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary. From Ibn Mas'ud: he saw what covered the lote-tree of the moths of gold; related by al-Mawardi. It was also said: he saw the Ascension. It was also said: it is what he saw that night on his journey, in his return and his beginning, and this is the best view. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 204]]. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verses 19–22:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ When He mentioned the revelation to the Prophet ﷺ and mentioned some of the signs of His power, He argued against the polytheists, for they worshipped that which has no intellect. He said (and it is said [في ب، ح، ز، س، ل، هـ: (وقيل).]): "Have you considered these deities you worship, or has anything been revealed to you as it was revealed to Muhammad?"

Al-Lat belonged to Thaqif, al-Uzza belonged to Quraysh and Banu Kinana, and Manat belonged to Banu Hudhayl [All copies of the original text agree that Manat belonged to Banu Hilal, and we have not seen this statement from anyone other than the author.]. Hisham said: Manat belonged to Hudhayl and Khuza'a. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and he demolished it in the year of the Conquest. Then they took al-Lat in al-Ta'if, and it was newer than Manat. It was a square rock, and its custodians (sadana, singular sadin: keepers of an idol) were from Thaqif. They had built a structure over it, and Quraysh and all the Arabs revered it. By it the Arabs would name Zayd al-Lat and Taym al-Lat. It was located at the place of the left minaret [The addition is from the Kitab al-Asnam of Ibn al-Kalbi.] of the mosque of al-Ta'if. It remained so until Thaqif embraced Islam, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, who demolished it and burned it with fire.

Then they took al-Uzza, which was newer than al-Lat. Zalim ibn As'ad took it, and it was in the valley of Nakhla al-Shamiyya above Dhat 'Irq. They built a house over it, and they would hear a voice from it [In the Kitab al-Asnam: "fihi" (in it) instead of "minha" (from it).]. Ibn Hisham said: My father narrated to me from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, who said: al-Uzza was a female devil who used to come to three acacia trees in the bottom of Nakhla. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "Go to the bottom of Nakhla, for you will find three acacia trees; cut down the first one." He went and cut it down. When he came back to him, he said: "Did you see anything?" He said: "No." He said: "Cut down the second one." He went and cut it down. Then he came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Did you see anything?" He said: "No." He said: "Cut down the third one." Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 23–26:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are nothing but names that you have named﴾, meaning: they are not (anything), i.e. these idols; (nothing but names you have named), meaning: you carved them and named them gods.

(You and your fathers) meaning: you imitated them in that.

(For which God has sent down no authority) meaning: God has not sent down for them any proof or evidence.

(They follow nothing but conjecture) he shifts from address (khitab) to narrative (khabar), meaning: these people follow nothing but conjecture.

(And what the souls desire) meaning: what they incline toward. The common reading is (yattabi'una) with the ya'. ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr, Ayyub and Ibn al-Sumaiqaʿ read (tattabi'una) with the ta', in address (khitab). This is also the reading of Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas.

(And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance) meaning: the clarification from the Messenger that they are not gods.

(Or does man have whatever he wishes?) meaning: whatever he desires. That is, it is not his. It was said: (Does man have whatever he wishes) of sons, meaning that it be his alone and not daughters. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) without recompense? The matter is not so. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) of prophethood, that it be in him rather than others. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) of the intercession of the idols; it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It was said: it concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was said: it concerns all the disbelievers.

(So to God belong the Hereafter and the first life) He gives to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills; not whatever anyone wishes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And how many an angel there is in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all, except after God gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾. This is a rebuke from God, the Exalted, to those who worship the angels and the idols and claim that this brings them closer to God, the Exalted. So He informs that the angels, despite the abundance of their worship and their honour before God, do not intercede except for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for. Al-Akhfash said: "malak" (angel) is singular in form but collective in meaning, like His saying, the Exalted: (none of you could withhold him from Us) [see vol. 18, p. 276]. It was also said: He mentioned one angel only because "kam" (how many) indicates plurality.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They are nothing but names that you have named﴾, meaning: they are not (anything), i.e. these idols; (nothing but names you have named), meaning: you carved them and named them gods.

(You and your fathers) meaning: you imitated them in that.

(For which God has sent down no authority) meaning: God has not sent down for them any proof or evidence.

(They follow nothing but conjecture) he shifts from address (khitab) to narrative (khabar), meaning: these people follow nothing but conjecture.

(And what the souls desire) meaning: what they incline toward. The common reading is (yattabi'una) with the ya'. ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr, Ayyub and Ibn al-Sumaiqaʿ read (tattabi'una) with the ta', in address (khitab). This is also the reading of Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas.

(And there has certainly come to them from their Lord the guidance) meaning: the clarification from the Messenger that they are not gods.

(Or does man have whatever he wishes?) meaning: whatever he desires. That is, it is not his. It was said: (Does man have whatever he wishes) of sons, meaning that it be his alone and not daughters. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) without recompense? The matter is not so. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) of prophethood, that it be in him rather than others. It was said: (Or does man have whatever he wishes) of the intercession of the idols; it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. It was said: it concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. It was said: it concerns all the disbelievers.

(So to God belong the Hereafter and the first life) He gives to whom He wills and withholds from whom He wills; not whatever anyone wishes.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And how many an angel there is in the heavens whose intercession will not avail at all, except after God gives permission to whom He wills and approves﴾. This is a rebuke from God, the Exalted, to those who worship the angels and the idols and claim that this brings them closer to God, the Exalted. So He informs that the angels, despite the abundance of their worship and their honour before God, do not intercede except for one whom He has permitted to be interceded for. Al-Akhfash said: "malak" (angel) is singular in form but collective in meaning, like His saying, the Exalted: (none of you could withhold him from Us) [see vol. 18, p. 276]. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verses 27–30:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ are the disbelievers who said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah," and "The idols are the daughters of Allah."

(They name the angels with the name of females) meaning, by naming them as females; that is, they believe that the angels are females and that they are the daughters of Allah.

(And they have no knowledge of it) meaning: they did not witness His creation of the angels, they did not hear what they claimed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they did not read it in any book.

(They follow only assumption) meaning: they follow nothing but conjecture regarding the claim that the angels are females.

(And assumption does not avail against the truth at all).

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ meaning: the Qur'an and faith. This verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf).

(And he desires nothing but the worldly life) It was revealed concerning al-Nadr (ibn al-Harith). It is also said: concerning al-Walid (ibn al-Mughira).

(That is the extent of their knowledge) meaning: they only perceive the affairs of their worldly life, and they are ignorant of the affairs of their religion. Al-Farra' said: He belittled them and looked down upon them; that is, this is the measure of their intellects and the extent of their knowledge, that they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter. It is also said: it refers to their making the angels and the idols daughters of Allah.

(Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way) meaning: who has deviated from His religion, (and He is most knowing of who is guided). So He will recompense each of them according to their deeds.

It is also said: it refers to their making the angels and the idols daughters of Allah.

(Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way) meaning: who has deviated from His religion, (and He is most knowing of who is guided). So He will recompense each of them according to their deeds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, so that He may repay those who did evil for what they did and repay those who did good with the best (reward)﴾. The *lam* in *liyajziya* (so that He may repay) is connected to the meaning indicated by ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, as if He said: He is the owner of that; He guides whom He wills and leads astray whom He wills, so that He may repay the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. It was also said that ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a parenthetical interjection in the speech, and the meaning is: Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided, so that He may repay. It was also said that it is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), meaning: and the consequence of the affair of creation is that among them there will be the evildoer and the doer of good. So for the evildoer is the evil end (*al-su'a*), which is Hell, and for the doer of good is the best (*al-husna*), which is Paradise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿who avoid the major sins and immoralities﴾. This is a description of the doers of good, meaning they do not commit the major sins (*kaba'ir al-ithm*), which is shirk, because it is the greatest of sins. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *kabira* (singular) instead of *kaba'ira*, and Ibn 'Abbas explained it as shirk.

"Immoralities" (*al-fawahish*) refers to adultery (*al-zina*). Muqatil said: "major sins" (*kaba'ir al-ithm*) is every sin that is sealed with the Fire.

"Immoralities" is every sin that carries a prescribed penalty (*hadd*). This matter has already been discussed in *al-Nisa'* [See vol. 5, p. 158].

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), and this is the second issue. He said: ﴿except for minor lapses (*al-lamam*)﴾, which are the minor sins that no one is safe from falling into except one whom Allah protects and preserves. The meaning of *al-lamam* has been disputed. Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: *al-lamam* is everything short of adultery.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a man called Nabhan the Date-Seller, who had a shop in which he sold dates. A woman came to him to buy dates, and he said to her: "What is inside the storeroom is better than this." When she entered, he made advances to her, but she refused and left. Nabhan regretted it, and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! There is nothing a man does except that I have done it, except intercourse." He said: "Perhaps (her husband is a warrior (*ghazin*))." Then this verse was revealed. This has been mentioned at the end of *Hud* [See vol. 9, p. 111, where a different narration clarifies the vagueness of this report].

Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Hudhayfah and Masruq also said: *al-lamam* is what falls short of sexual intercourse: kissing, touching, looking, and lying together.

Masruq narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The adultery of the eyes is looking, the adultery of the hands is grasping, the adultery of the feet is walking, and the private parts either confirm that or deny it. If it goes forward, it is adultery, and if it stops short, it is *lamam*."

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more resembling *al-lamam* than what Abu Hurayrah said: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eyes is looking, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private parts confirm that or deny it.'"

The meaning is that the grave immorality and the complete adultery that entails the prescribed penalty (*hadd*) in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter is in the private parts, while other things have a share of sin.

And Allah knows best.

In the narration of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His share of adultery is written for the son of Adam, which will inevitably reach him. The adultery of the two eyes is looking, the adultery of the two ears is listening, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the adultery of the hand is grasping, the adultery of the foot is walking, and the heart desires and wishes, and the private parts confirm that or deny it." Muslim recorded it.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned the hadith of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, in which he mentioned the ear, the hand and the foot, and added after the eyes and the tongue: "and the adultery of the two lips is kissing." This is one opinion.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is a man who commits a sin and then repents. He said: "Did you not hear the Prophet (ﷺ) saying:

If Allah forgives, He forgives much,
and which servant of Yours does not commit sin?"

This was narrated by 'Amr ibn Dinar from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. [Al-Tirmidhi narrated this hadith with this chain and said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."] Al-Nahhas said: "This is the most authentic thing said about it, and the most exalted in its chain."

Shu'bah narrated from Mansur from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿except for minor lapses﴾: he said: it is that a servant commits a sin and then does not return to it. The poet said [it is Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, who said it at the time of death]:

If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
and which servant of Yours does not commit sin?

Mujahid and al-Hasan also said the same: it is one who commits a sin and then does not return to it. Similar is reported from al-Zuhri, who said: *al-lamam* is that a person commits adultery and then repents and does not return to it, or steals or drinks wine, then repents and does not return to it.

The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾, up to the end of the verse [See vol. 4, pp. 209 and 215]. Then He said: ﴿Those, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord﴾ [See vol. 4, pp. 209 and 215], so He guaranteed them forgiveness, just as He said after *al-lamam*: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾. According to this interpretation, ﴿except for minor lapses﴾ is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*).

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: *al-lamam* is what falls short of shirk.

It was also said: *al-lamam* is a sin between the two prescribed penalties, meaning what has not received a prescribed penalty in this world, nor has a punishment been threatened for it in the Hereafter, and it is expiated by the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn Zayd, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Al-'Awfi and al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Kalbi said: *al-lamam* has two aspects. The first is every sin for which Allah has not mentioned a prescribed penalty in this world or a punishment in the Hereafter, and this is what the five daily prayers expiate, so long as it does not reach the major sins and immoralities. The other aspect is a great sin that a person commits once and again, and then repents from it.

From Ibn 'Abbas also, and from Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Thabit: *al-lamam* is what occurred in the pre-Islamic period, so He will not hold them accountable for it. This is because the polytheists said to the Muslims: "You were only yesterday doing (these things) with us," and so this was revealed. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son [in A: "and his father," but what we have recorded agrees with the *Tafsir* of Abu Hayyan and al-Tabari] said this, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [See vol. 5, p. 116].

It was also said: *al-lamam* is that one commits a sin that was not his habit. This was said by Niftawayh, who said: The Arabs say: "He does not come to us except *lamaman*," meaning from time to time. He said: It cannot be *alamma* (to come near to) without doing it, because the Arabs do not say *alamma bina* (he visited us) except when the person actually does it, not when he merely intends it and does not do it.

In the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): *alamma al-rajul* (the man committed *lamam*), which is minor sins, and it is said: it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Someone other than al-Jawhari recited:

Visit Zaynab before the caravan departs,
and say: If you are cold toward us, the heart has not grown weary.

Meaning: draw near.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: *al-lamam* is the soul's habit of occasional returns. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is what passes over the heart, meaning occurs to it. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: whatever you intend, whether good or evil, is *lamam*.

The evidence for this interpretation is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The devil has a touch (*lamma*) and the angel has a touch." The hadith is long. It has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 3, p. 329], at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The devil threatens you with poverty﴾.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the root of *lamam* and *ilmam* is what a person does once and again, without going deep into it or persisting in it. It is said: "I visited (*alamma*) him," when one visits and departs from him. And it is said: "I did not do it except *lamaman* and *ilmaman*," meaning from time to time. "Your visit is merely *ilmam*," and from this is *ilmam al-khayal* (the passing of an apparition), as al-A'sha said:

A passing apparition from Qutaylah, after
her rope had grown weak from our rope and was cut off.

It was also said: *illa* (except) here means *waw* (and). Al-Farra' denied this and said: the meaning is "except what is close to small sins."

It was said: *al-lamam* is the glance that happens suddenly. I say: This is far-fetched, because it is pardoned at the outset and is not held against one, since it occurs without intention or choice. Its explanation has already been given in *al-Nur* [See vol. 12, p. 227].

*Al-lamam* also means a touch of madness; a man who is *malmum* has a *lamam*. It is also said: a *lammah* from the jinn struck so-and-so, meaning a touch and a small amount. A poet said:

So when that, O Kubaysha, was not
except like the touch of a dreamer with a phantom.

[The *waw* in *wa-dhalika* is extra, as in the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

So when that, its time, is nothing but its time,
and when something has passed, it is as if it never happened.]

The third issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾, to those who repent from their sin and seek forgiveness. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Maysarah 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, who was one of the eminent companions of Ibn Mas'ud, said: "I saw in a dream as if I had entered Paradise, and there were pavilions erected. I said: 'Whose are these?' They said: 'They belong to Dhu al-Kala' and Hawshab.' These two had killed one another. I said: 'How is that?' They said: 'Indeed they met Allah and found Him vast in forgiveness.'" Abu Khalid said: "It reached me that Dhu al-Kala' freed twelve thousand slave-girls."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾ [more than you know yourselves], ﴿when He produced you from the earth﴾, meaning your father Adam from clay. The address is in the plural form. Al-Tirmidhi Abu 'Abdullah said: "It is not so in our view. Rather, the production occurred from the dust that was lifted from the earth, and we were all in that dust and in that clay. Then the waters came out of the clay into the loins, along with the scattering of souls with their differing forms. Then He extracted them from their loins in differing forms: among them some are like shining pearls, some are brighter than others, some are black like coal, and some are blacker than others. So the production was directed at us and at him."

Isa ibn Hammad al-'Asqalani narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn Bakr narrated to us, saying: al-Awza'i narrated to us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first and the last were displayed before me, between my hands, in this chamber of mine tonight." Someone said: "O Messenger of Allah! And who has passed away of creation?" He said: "Yes. Adam was displayed before me, and whoever is below him. Was there ever any creature created (*ahad*)?" They said: "And who are those in the loins of men and the wombs of mothers?" He said: "Yes. They were shaped in clay, and I knew them, just as Adam was taught all the names."

I say: It has already been mentioned at the beginning of *al-An'am* [See vol. 6, p. 388] that every human being is created from the clay of the place in which he will be buried.

His saying, ﴿and when you were fetuses (*ajinnah*)﴾. *Janin* is the plural of *janin*, which is the child as long as it is in the womb. It is called *janin* because it is concealed and hidden. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

A she-camel of smooth skin and bright color, a virgin, you had not known a fetus [i.e., she had never carried a child in her womb].

Its first hemistich is: "My two forearms of a brown, white-skinned virgin."

Makhul said: "We were fetuses in the wombs of our mothers. Some of us fell (miscarried), and we were among those who remained. Then we became infants at the breast, and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became youths (yafa'a), and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became young men, and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became old men, may you have no father! So what are we waiting for after this?"

Ibn Lahi'a narrated from al-Harith ibn Yazid, from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews used to say, when a young child of theirs died, 'He is a truthful one (siddiq).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: '(The) Jews have lied. There is no soul (nasamah) that Allah creates in its mother's womb except that it is either wretched or happy.' Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed at that point this verse: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾ to its end." A similar report has come from Aisha, with the words "The Jews..." and the like.

﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾, i.e., do not praise them and do not commend them, for that is further from showing off (riya') and closer to humility (khushu').

﴿He knows best who is righteous﴾, i.e., who has made his deed sincere and guarded himself against the punishment of Allah, related from al-Hasan and others. Al-Hasan said: "Allah, glorified is He, has informed every soul of what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning." The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in (Surat) al-Nisa', at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who justify themselves?﴾ [Vol. 5, p. 246]; reflect on it there. Ibn Abbas said: "There is no one from this Ummah whom I would commend except the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And Allah knows best.

It was also said that it is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), meaning: and the consequence of the affair of creation is that among them there will be the evildoer and the doer of good. So for the evildoer is the evil end (*al-su'a*), which is Hell, and for the doer of good is the best (*al-husna*), which is Paradise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who avoid the major sins and immoralities, except for minor lapses﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿who avoid the major sins and immoralities﴾. This is a description of the doers of good, meaning they do not commit the major sins (*kaba'ir al-ithm*), which is shirk, because it is the greatest of sins. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *kabira* (singular) instead of *kaba'ira*, and Ibn 'Abbas explained it as shirk.

"Immoralities" (*al-fawahish*) refers to adultery (*al-zina*). Muqatil said: "major sins" (*kaba'ir al-ithm*) is every sin that is sealed with the Fire.

"Immoralities" is every sin that carries a prescribed penalty (*hadd*). This matter has already been discussed in *al-Nisa'* [See vol. 5, p. 158].

Then He made an exception, a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), and this is the second issue. He said: ﴿except for minor lapses (*al-lamam*)﴾, which are the minor sins that no one is safe from falling into except one whom Allah protects and preserves. The meaning of *al-lamam* has been disputed. Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sha'bi said: *al-lamam* is everything short of adultery.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning a man called Nabhan the Date-Seller, who had a shop in which he sold dates. A woman came to him to buy dates, and he said to her: "What is inside the storeroom is better than this." When she entered, he made advances to her, but she refused and left. Nabhan regretted it, and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah! There is nothing a man does except that I have done it, except intercourse." He said: "Perhaps (her husband is a warrior (*ghazin*))." Then this verse was revealed. This has been mentioned at the end of *Hud* [See vol. 9, p. 111, where a different narration clarifies the vagueness of this report].

Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Hudhayfah and Masruq also said: *al-lamam* is what falls short of sexual intercourse: kissing, touching, looking, and lying together.

Masruq narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The adultery of the eyes is looking, the adultery of the hands is grasping, the adultery of the feet is walking, and the private parts either confirm that or deny it. If it goes forward, it is adultery, and if it stops short, it is *lamam*."

In the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari and Muslim, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I have not seen anything more resembling *al-lamam* than what Abu Hurayrah said: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of adultery, which he will inevitably encounter. The adultery of the eyes is looking, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and longs, and the private parts confirm that or deny it.'"

The meaning is that the grave immorality and the complete adultery that entails the prescribed penalty (*hadd*) in this world and the punishment in the Hereafter is in the private parts, while other things have a share of sin.

And Allah knows best.

In the narration of Abu Salih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His share of adultery is written for the son of Adam, which will inevitably reach him. The adultery of the two eyes is looking, the adultery of the two ears is listening, the adultery of the tongue is speech, the adultery of the hand is grasping, the adultery of the foot is walking, and the heart desires and wishes, and the private parts confirm that or deny it." Muslim recorded it.

Al-Tha'labi mentioned the hadith of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, in which he mentioned the ear, the hand and the foot, and added after the eyes and the tongue: "and the adultery of the two lips is kissing." This is one opinion.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is a man who commits a sin and then repents. He said: "Did you not hear the Prophet (ﷺ) saying:

If Allah forgives, He forgives much,
and which servant of Yours does not commit sin?"

This was narrated by 'Amr ibn Dinar from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas. [Al-Tirmidhi narrated this hadith with this chain and said: "This is a hasan sahih gharib hadith."] Al-Nahhas said: "This is the most authentic thing said about it, and the most exalted in its chain."

Shu'bah narrated from Mansur from Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿except for minor lapses﴾: he said: it is that a servant commits a sin and then does not return to it. The poet said [it is Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt, who said it at the time of death]:

If You forgive, O Allah, You forgive much,
and which servant of Yours does not commit sin?

Mujahid and al-Hasan also said the same: it is one who commits a sin and then does not return to it. Similar is reported from al-Zuhri, who said: *al-lamam* is that a person commits adultery and then repents and does not return to it, or steals or drinks wine, then repents and does not return to it.

The evidence for this interpretation is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾, up to the end of the verse [See vol. 4, pp. 209 and 215]. Then He said: ﴿Those, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord﴾ [See vol. 4, pp. 209 and 215], so He guaranteed them forgiveness, just as He said after *al-lamam*: ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾. According to this interpretation, ﴿except for minor lapses﴾ is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*).

'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said: *al-lamam* is what falls short of shirk.

It was also said: *al-lamam* is a sin between the two prescribed penalties, meaning what has not received a prescribed penalty in this world, nor has a punishment been threatened for it in the Hereafter, and it is expiated by the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn Zayd, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Qatadah. Al-'Awfi and al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Kalbi said: *al-lamam* has two aspects. The first is every sin for which Allah has not mentioned a prescribed penalty in this world or a punishment in the Hereafter, and this is what the five daily prayers expiate, so long as it does not reach the major sins and immoralities. The other aspect is a great sin that a person commits once and again, and then repents from it.

From Ibn 'Abbas also, and from Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Thabit: *al-lamam* is what occurred in the pre-Islamic period, so He will not hold them accountable for it. This is because the polytheists said to the Muslims: "You were only yesterday doing (these things) with us," and so this was revealed. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son [in A: "and his father," but what we have recorded agrees with the *Tafsir* of Abu Hayyan and al-Tabari] said this, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ [See vol. 5, p. 116].

It was also said: *al-lamam* is that one commits a sin that was not his habit. This was said by Niftawayh, who said: The Arabs say: "He does not come to us except *lamaman*," meaning from time to time. He said: It cannot be *alamma* (to come near to) without doing it, because the Arabs do not say *alamma bina* (he visited us) except when the person actually does it, not when he merely intends it and does not do it.

In the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): *alamma al-rajul* (the man committed *lamam*), which is minor sins, and it is said: it is approaching disobedience without actually committing it. Someone other than al-Jawhari recited:

Visit Zaynab before the caravan departs,
and say: If you are cold toward us, the heart has not grown weary.

Meaning: draw near.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: *al-lamam* is the soul's habit of occasional returns. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is what passes over the heart, meaning occurs to it. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: whatever you intend, whether good or evil, is *lamam*.

The evidence for this interpretation is his (ﷺ) saying, peace be upon him: "The devil has a touch (*lamma*) and the angel has a touch." The hadith is long. It has already been discussed in *al-Baqarah* [See vol. 3, p. 329], at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The devil threatens you with poverty﴾.

Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the root of *lamam* and *ilmam* is what a person does once and again, without going deep into it or persisting in it. It is said: "I visited (*alamma*) him," when one visits and departs from him. And it is said: "I did not do it except *lamaman* and *ilmaman*," meaning from time to time. "Your visit is merely *ilmam*," and from this is *ilmam al-khayal* (the passing of an apparition), as al-A'sha said:

A passing apparition from Qutaylah, after
her rope had grown weak from our rope and was cut off.

It was also said: *illa* (except) here means *waw* (and). Al-Farra' denied this and said: the meaning is "except what is close to small sins."

It was said: *al-lamam* is the glance that happens suddenly. I say: This is far-fetched, because it is pardoned at the outset and is not held against one, since it occurs without intention or choice. Its explanation has already been given in *al-Nur* [See vol. 12, p. 227].

*Al-lamam* also means a touch of madness; a man who is *malmum* has a *lamam*. It is also said: a *lammah* from the jinn struck so-and-so, meaning a touch and a small amount. A poet said:

So when that, O Kubaysha, was not
except like the touch of a dreamer with a phantom.

[The *waw* in *wa-dhalika* is extra, as in the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

So when that, its time, is nothing but its time,
and when something has passed, it is as if it never happened.]

The third issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾, to those who repent from their sin and seek forgiveness. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Maysarah 'Amr ibn Shurahbil, who was one of the eminent companions of Ibn Mas'ud, said: "I saw in a dream as if I had entered Paradise, and there were pavilions erected. I said: 'Whose are these?' They said: 'They belong to Dhu al-Kala' and Hawshab.' These two had killed one another. I said: 'How is that?' They said: 'Indeed they met Allah and found Him vast in forgiveness.'" Abu Khalid said: "It reached me that Dhu al-Kala' freed twelve thousand slave-girls."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knows you best﴾ [more than you know yourselves], ﴿when He produced you from the earth﴾, meaning your father Adam from clay. The address is in the plural form. Al-Tirmidhi Abu 'Abdullah said: "It is not so in our view. Rather, the production occurred from the dust that was lifted from the earth, and we were all in that dust and in that clay. Then the waters came out of the clay into the loins, along with the scattering of souls with their differing forms. Then He extracted them from their loins in differing forms: among them some are like shining pearls, some are brighter than others, some are black like coal, and some are blacker than others. So the production was directed at us and at him."

Isa ibn Hammad al-'Asqalani narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn Bakr narrated to us, saying: al-Awza'i narrated to us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first and the last were displayed before me, between my hands, in this chamber of mine tonight." Someone said: "O Messenger of Allah! And who has passed away of creation?" He said: "Yes. Adam was displayed before me, and whoever is below him. Was there ever any creature created (*ahad*)?" They said: "And who are those in the loins of men and the wombs of mothers?" He said: "Yes. They were shaped in clay, and I knew them, just as Adam was taught all the names."

I say: It has already been mentioned at the beginning of *al-An'am* [See vol. 6, p. 388] that every human being is created from the clay of the place in which he will be buried.

His saying, ﴿and when you were fetuses (*ajinnah*)﴾. *Janin* is the plural of *janin*, which is the child as long as it is in the womb. It is called *janin* because it is concealed and hidden. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

A she-camel of smooth skin and bright color, a virgin, you had not known a fetus [i.e., she had never carried a child in her womb].

Its first hemistich is: "My two forearms of a brown, white-skinned virgin."

Makhul said: "We were fetuses in the wombs of our mothers. Some of us fell (miscarried), and we were among those who remained. Then we became infants at the breast, and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became youths (yafa'a), and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became young men, and some of us perished, and we were among those who remained. Then we became old men, may you have no father! So what are we waiting for after this?"

Ibn Lahi'a narrated from al-Harith ibn Yazid, from Thabit ibn al-Harith al-Ansari, who said: "The Jews used to say, when a young child of theirs died, 'He is a truthful one (siddiq).' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: '(The) Jews have lied. There is no soul (nasamah) that Allah creates in its mother's womb except that it is either wretched or happy.' Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed at that point this verse: ﴿He knows you best, since He produced you from the earth﴾ to its end." A similar report has come from Aisha, with the words "The Jews..." and the like.

﴿So do not justify yourselves﴾, i.e., do not praise them and do not commend them, for that is further from showing off (riya') and closer to humility (khushu').

﴿He knows best who is righteous﴾, i.e., who has made his deed sincere and guarded himself against the punishment of Allah, related from al-Hasan and others. Al-Hasan said: "Allah, glorified is He, has informed every soul of what it is doing, what it is producing, and to what it is returning." The discussion of the meaning of this verse has already passed in (Surat) al-Nisa', at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen those who justify themselves?﴾ [Vol. 5, p. 246]; reflect on it there. Ibn Abbas said: "There is no one from this Ummah whom I would commend except the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 53, verses 33–35:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away, and gave a little, and then withheld?﴾ [the verses [[from b, w, l.]]] When He made clear the ignorance of the polytheists in worshipping idols, He mentioned one of them specifically, for his evil deed. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, so some of the polytheists reproached him and said: "Why did you abandon the religion of the elders and misguide them? And you claim that they are in the Fire?" He said: "I feared the punishment of Allah." So he (the polytheist) guaranteed him that if he gave him some of his wealth and returned to his polytheism, he would bear the punishment of Allah on his behalf. So he gave the one who had reproached him some of what he had guaranteed [[the addition is from Asbab al-Nuzul (occasions of revelation) by al-Wahidi.]] Then he became stingy and withheld it, and Allah revealed this verse.

Muqatil said: al-Walid had praised the Qur'an, then withdrew from it, so this was revealed: (and gave a little), that is, of good with his tongue, (and then withheld), that is, he cut that off and held back from it.

It is also related from him that he gave the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a pledge of faith, then turned away, so this was revealed: (Have you seen the one who turned away?), the verse.

Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and al-Musayyib ibn Sharik said: It was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), who used to give charity and spend in good causes. His foster brother, Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh, said to him: "What is this that you are doing? Soon nothing will remain for you." Uthman said: "I have sins and wrongdoings, and by what I do I seek the pleasure of Allah the Exalted and hope for His forgiveness." Abdullah said to him: "Give me your she-camel with its saddle, and I will bear all your sins for you." So he gave it to him and had witnesses to it, and he held back from some of the charity he used to give. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: (Have you seen the one who turned away, and gave a little, and then withheld?). So Uthman returned to the best and most beautiful of that (practice). Al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi mentioned this.

al-Suddi also said: It was revealed concerning al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, because he would sometimes agree with the Prophet (ﷺ).

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: It was revealed concerning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. He said: "By Allah, Muhammad only commands noble character," and this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and gave a little, and then withheld﴾.

Al-Dahhak said: He is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five she-camels to a poor man among the Emigrants when he apostatised from his religion, and guaranteed to bear on his behalf the sin of his return.

The origin of (akda) is from al-kudya (hard rock). It is said of one who digs a well and reaches a rock in which digging is not possible for him: "He has akda (been stopped)." Then the Arabs used it for one who gives but does not complete, and for one who seeks something but does not reach its end. al-Hutay'a said:

*"He gave a little, then withheld his gift,*
*and whoever gives kindness among people is praised."*

al-Kisa'i and others said: akda al-hafir and ajbal, when the digger reaches in his digging a hard rock or a mountain, so he cannot dig further. And "hafara fa-akda" means when he reaches solid ground. It is said: "His fingers were kadiyat" when they grew weary from digging. "His hand kadiyat" when it grew weary and did nothing. "Akda al-nabt" when its produce became little. "Kadat al-ardu takdu kadwan [wa kuduwan]" and it is "kadiya" when its plants were slow to grow, from Abu Zayd. "Akdaytu al-rajul 'an al-shay'" means I turned him back from it. "Akda al-rajul" means when his goodness became little. And His saying: (and gave a little, and then withheld) means he cut off the little.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen, so that he sees?﴾ That is: does this stingy one have knowledge of what is hidden from him of the matter of punishment?

(so that he sees) means he knows what is hidden from him of the matter of the Hereafter, and of what will happen in his affair, so that he would guarantee bearing the punishment on behalf of another. And this is enough as proof of ignorance and folly. This sense of "seeing" is the one that takes two objects, and both objects are omitted, as if He had said: "so that he sees the unseen as he sees the witnessed."

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah read (wafa) lightly, and its meaning is "he was truthful in his speech and his deeds." It returns to the meaning of the reading of the majority, (waffa) with shaddah, that is, he performed all that was obligated upon him and omitted nothing from it. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he stood by the condition of what he claimed, because Allah, Most High, said to him: ﴿Submit, he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ (see vol. 2, p. 98 and p. 134), so Allah demanded of him the validity of his claim, and tested him in his wealth, his children and himself, and found him fulfilling that. This is His saying: ﴿and Abraham who fulfilled﴾, that is, he claimed Islam and then validated his claim.

It was also said: he fulfilled his practice every day with four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day, narrated by al-Haytham from Abu Umamah from the Prophet ﷺ. Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi narrated from his father: "Shall I not inform you why Allah, Most High, named His friend Abraham ﴿who fulfilled﴾? Because he used to say every morning and evening: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ (see vol. 14, p. 14)" to the end of the verse. Sahl ibn Mu'adh narrated it from Anas from his father from the Prophet ﷺ.

It was also said: (wafa) means he fulfilled what he was sent with, which is His saying: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. Ibn Abbas said: before Abraham, peace be upon him, they would hold a man accountable for the sin of another, and they would take a guardian for a guardian in killing and wounding, so a man would be killed for his father, his son, his brother, his paternal uncle, his maternal uncle, his cousin, his relative, his wife, her husband, and his slave. Abraham, peace be upon him, conveyed from Allah, Most High: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

This is the best (view), because it is general. Likewise Mujahid said: (wafa) with what was obligated upon him. Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: His saying, Most High, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ up to His saying: ﴿then which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ is in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses. The discussion of ﴿and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has already passed in full at the end of al-An'am (see vol. 7, p. 157 and p. 215).

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is abrogated by His saying, Most High: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in belief - We will join them with their descendants﴾ (see p. 66 of this part). So the child will be placed in the scale of his father on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah, Most High, will grant the fathers intercession for the children and the children for the fathers. His saying, Most High, indicates this: ﴿Your fathers and your sons - you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 74).

Most of the people of interpretation said: it is muhkamah (not abrogated), and no one's deed benefits another. They agreed that no one prays on behalf of another. Malik did not permit fasting, Hajj or charity on behalf of the dead, except that he said: if he bequeathed the Hajj and died, it is permissible that Hajj be performed on his behalf. Al-Shafi'i and others permitted voluntary Hajj on behalf of the dead. It is narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she performed i'tikaf on behalf of her brother Abd al-Rahman and freed (a slave) on his behalf. It is narrated that Sa'd ibn Ubadah said to the Prophet ﷺ: "My mother has died; shall I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Which charity is best?" He said: "Giving water to drink." All of this has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah (see vol. 3, p. 428), Al 'Imran (see vol. 4, p. 151) and al-A'raf (the text here reads thus in the manuscripts, and we have not found this meaning in the mentioned surah).

It has been said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only said: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾, and the lam of genitive in Arabic means ownership and obligation. So it is not obligatory for man except what he strove for. If someone gives charity on his behalf, nothing becomes obligatory for him, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestows upon him what is not obligatory for him, just as He bestows upon children by admitting them to Paradise without deed. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾ means the disbeliever; as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf.

I say: Many hadiths indicate this view, that the believer reaches the reward of righteous deeds from others. Many of them have already been mentioned, for whoever reflects on them. There is no disagreement regarding charity, as in the beginning of the Book of Muslim, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak. In the Sahih: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three," and in it: "or a righteous child who supplicates for him." All of this is a bounty from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as the multiplication of rewards is a bounty from Him. He records for them one good deed as ten up to seven hundred times, up to a thousand thousand good deeds. As was said to Abu Hurairah: "Did you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Allah rewards one good deed with a thousand thousand good deeds'?" He said: "I heard him say: 'Allah rewards one good deed with two thousand thousand good deeds.'" This is a bounty. The way of justice is ﴿that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾.

I say: It is possible that His saying, ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾, is specific to the evil deed, by the evidence of what is in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurairah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: When My servant intends a good deed and does not do it, I record it for him as one good deed; if he does it, I record it for him as ten good deeds up to seven hundred times. Al-Akhfash said: one says "jazaytuhu al-jaza'" and "jazaytuhu bil-jaza'," both the same with no difference between them. The poet said:

If I repay Alqamah ibn Sa'd for his striving, I will not repay him for the trial of a single day.

So he combined the two usages.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾, that is, the return, the destination and the final place, where He punishes and rewards. It was said: from Him is the beginning of the favor, and to Him is the end of security. It is narrated from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah, Most High, is mentioned, then stop."

I say: From this meaning is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Satan comes to one of you and says: 'Who created such-and-such?' until he says to him: 'Who created your Lord?' When he reaches that, let him seek refuge in Allah and let him stop." It has already passed at the end of al-A'raf (see vol. 7, p. 348). And well did the one who said:

Do not reflect upon the Exalted One, may His face be mighty, for you will perish if you do so and be forsaken.

Rather, His creations are before you, so take heed from them, and say what the noble friend said.
