He singled out the scriptures of Abraham and Moses for mention because between Noah and Abraham a man would be held accountable for the offense of his brother, his son and his father. This was said by al-Hudhayl ibn Shurahbil.

(And) this (anna) is the light form of the heavy (anna), and its position is in the genitive, as a substitute for (ma), or it may be in the nominative position by implying "huwa" (it). Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah read (wafa) lightly, and its meaning is "he was truthful in his speech and his deeds." It returns to the meaning of the reading of the majority, (waffa) with shaddah, that is, he performed all that was obligated upon him and omitted nothing from it. It has already passed in al-Baqarah (see vol. 2, p. 98 and p. 134) at His saying, Most High: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with commands, and he fulfilled them﴾, and at-tawfiyah is completion. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: he stood by the condition of what he claimed, because Allah, Most High, said to him: ﴿Submit, he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds"﴾ (see vol. 2, p. 98 and p. 134), so Allah demanded of him the validity of his claim, and tested him in his wealth, his children and himself, and found him fulfilling that. This is His saying: ﴿and Abraham who fulfilled﴾, that is, he claimed Islam and then validated his claim.

It was also said: he fulfilled his practice every day with four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day, narrated by al-Haytham from Abu Umamah from the Prophet ﷺ. Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi narrated from his father: "Shall I not inform you why Allah, Most High, named His friend Abraham ﴿who fulfilled﴾? Because he used to say every morning and evening: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ (see vol. 14, p. 14)" to the end of the verse. Sahl ibn Mu'adh narrated it from Anas from his father from the Prophet ﷺ.

It was also said: (wafa) means he fulfilled what he was sent with, which is His saying: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. Ibn Abbas said: before Abraham, peace be upon him, they would hold a man accountable for the sin of another, and they would take a guardian for a guardian in killing and wounding, so a man would be killed for his father, his son, his brother, his paternal uncle, his maternal uncle, his cousin, his relative, his wife, her husband, and his slave. Abraham, peace be upon him, conveyed from Allah, Most High: ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said regarding His saying, Most High, (wafa): he acted by what he was commanded and conveyed the messages of his Lord. This is the best (view), because it is general. Likewise Mujahid said: (wafa) with what was obligated upon him. Abu Malik al-Ghifari said: His saying, Most High, ﴿that no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ up to His saying: ﴿then which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ is in the scriptures of Abraham and Moses. The discussion of ﴿and no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾ has already passed in full at the end of al-An'am (see vol. 7, p. 157 and p. 215).

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that it is abrogated by His saying, Most High: ﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in belief - We will join them with their descendants﴾ (see p. 66 of this part). So the child will be placed in the scale of his father on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah, Most High, will grant the fathers intercession for the children and the children for the fathers. His saying, Most High, indicates this: ﴿Your fathers and your sons - you do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit﴾ (see vol. 5, p. 74).

Most of the people of interpretation said: it is muhkamah (not abrogated), and no one's deed benefits another. They agreed that no one prays on behalf of another. Malik did not permit fasting, Hajj or charity on behalf of the dead, except that he said: if he bequeathed the Hajj and died, it is permissible that Hajj be performed on his behalf. Al-Shafi'i and others permitted voluntary Hajj on behalf of the dead. It is narrated from Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she performed i'tikaf on behalf of her brother Abd al-Rahman and freed (a slave) on his behalf. It is narrated that Sa'd ibn Ubadah said to the Prophet ﷺ: "My mother has died; shall I give charity on her behalf?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Which charity is best?" He said: "Giving water to drink." All of this has already been discussed fully in al-Baqarah (see vol. 3, p. 428), Al 'Imran (see vol. 4, p. 151) and al-A'raf (the text here reads thus in the manuscripts, and we have not found this meaning in the mentioned surah).

It has been said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only said: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾, and the lam of genitive in Arabic means ownership and obligation. So it is not obligatory for man except what he strove for. If someone gives charity on his behalf, nothing becomes obligatory for him, but Allah, Mighty and Majestic, bestows upon him what is not obligatory for him, just as He bestows upon children by admitting them to Paradise without deed. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾ means the disbeliever; as for the believer, he has what he strove for and what others strove for on his behalf.

I say: Many hadiths indicate this view, that the believer reaches the reward of righteous deeds from others. Many of them have already been mentioned, for whoever reflects on them. There is no disagreement regarding charity, as in the beginning of the Book of Muslim, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak. In the Sahih: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three," and in it: "or a righteous child who supplicates for him." All of this is a bounty from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, just as the multiplication of rewards is a bounty from Him. He records for them one good deed as ten up to seven hundred times, up to a thousand thousand good deeds. As was said to Abu Hurairah: "Did you hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Allah rewards one good deed with a thousand thousand good deeds'?" He said: "I heard him say: 'Allah rewards one good deed with two thousand thousand good deeds.'" This is a bounty. The way of justice is ﴿that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾.

I say: It is possible that His saying, ﴿And that there is not for man except that for which he strives﴾, is specific to the evil deed, by the evidence of what is in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurairah from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: When My servant intends a good deed and does not do it, I record it for him as one good deed; if he does it, I record it for him as ten good deeds up to seven hundred times. And when he intends an evil deed and does not do it, I do not record it against him; if he does it, I record it as one evil deed."

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: ﴿except that for which he strives﴾ means except that which he intended. Its explanation is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "People will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection according to their intentions."

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that his striving will be seen﴾, that is, Allah, Most High, will show him his recompense on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾, that is, he will be repaid with it. Al-Akhfash said: one says "jazaytuhu al-jaza'" and "jazaytuhu bil-jaza'," both the same with no difference between them. The poet said:

If I repay Alqamah ibn Sa'd for his striving, I will not repay him for the trial of a single day.

So he combined the two usages.

His saying, Most High: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾, that is, the return, the destination and the final place, where He punishes and rewards. It was said: from Him is the beginning of the favor, and to Him is the end of security. It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: the Prophet ﷺ said regarding His saying: ﴿And that to your Lord is the finality﴾: "Do not reflect upon the Lord." It is narrated from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah, Most High, is mentioned, then stop."

I say: From this meaning is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Satan comes to one of you and says: 'Who created such-and-such?' until he says to him: 'Who created your Lord?' When he reaches that, let him seek refuge in Allah and let him stop." It has already passed at the end of al-A'raf (see vol. 7, p. 348). And well did the one who said:

Do not reflect upon the Exalted One, may His face be mighty, for you will perish if you do so and be forsaken.

Rather, His creations are before you, so take heed from them, and say what the noble friend said.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 53, verse 43–46:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾. The intermediaries have departed and the realities remain with Allah, glorified and exalted; so there is no doer except Him. In Sahih Muslim, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "No, by Allah, the Messenger of Allah never said that the dead is punished for the weeping of anyone. Rather, he said: (Indeed, Allah increases the punishment of the disbeliever because of the weeping of his family, and indeed it is Allah who makes laugh and makes weep, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another)." And from her, she said: The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by some of his companions while they were laughing, and he said: (If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much). Then Gabriel came down to him and said: "O Muhammad! Indeed Allah says to you: (And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep)." So he returned to them and said: (I had not taken forty steps before Gabriel came to me and said: Go to these people and say to them, indeed Allah, the Most High, says: "It is He who makes laugh and makes weep"), meaning He decreed the causes of laughter and weeping. Ata ibn Abi Muslim said: it means He made happy and made sad, because joy brings laughter and sorrow brings weeping. It was said to Umar: Did the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laugh? He said: Yes! And by Allah, faith was firmer in their hearts than the lofty mountains. This meaning has already been mentioned in (al-Naml) [[See vol. 13 p. 175.]] and (al-Tawbah) [[See vol. 8 p. 217.]]. Al-Hasan said: Allah makes the people of Paradise laugh in Paradise, and makes the people of Hell weep in Hell. It was said: He makes whom He wills laugh in this world by gladdening him, and makes whom He wills weep by grieving him. Al-Dahhak: He makes the earth laugh with plants and makes the sky weep with rain. It was said: He makes the trees laugh with blossoms and makes the clouds weep with rains. Dhu al-Nun said: He makes the hearts of the believers and the gnostics laugh with the sun of His recognition, and makes the hearts of the disbelievers and the disobedient weep with the darkness of their denial and disobedience. Sahl ibn Abd Allah said: Allah makes the obedient laugh with mercy and makes the disobedient weep with wrath. Muhammad ibn Ali al-Tirmidhi said: He makes the believer laugh in the Hereafter and makes him weep in this world. Bassam ibn Abd Allah said: Allah makes their teeth laugh and makes their hearts weep. And he recited:

The tooth laughs while the insides burn...
and its laughter is only false and fabricated.

O how many a weeper with an eye that has no tears,
and how many a laugher with a tooth though he has no strength left.

It was said: Allah, the Most High, singled out man with laughing and weeping among all animals, and there is no animal other than man that laughs and weeps. It has been said that the monkey alone laughs and does not weep, and that the camel alone weeps and does not laugh. Yusuf ibn al-Husayn said: Tahir al-Maqdisi was asked: Do the angels laugh? He said: They have not laughed, nor has anyone below the Throne since Hell was created.

﴿And that it is He who causes death and gives life﴾, meaning He decreed the causes of death and life. It was said: He created death and life, as He said: ﴿Who created death and life﴾ [[See vol. 18 p. 206]]; this was said by Ibn Bahr. It was said: He causes the disbeliever to die through disbelief and gives life to the believer through faith. Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life...﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 78 and vol. 6 p. 418]], the verse. And He said: ﴿Only those who hear respond, and the dead, Allah will raise them﴾ as previously explained [[See vol. 7 p. 78 and vol. 6 p. 418]]. To this refers the saying of Ata: He causes death by His justice and gives life by His grace; and the saying of one who said: He causes death by withholding and miserliness and gives life by generosity and giving. It was said: He causes the drop to die and gives life to the soul. It was said: He causes the fathers to die and gives life to the sons. It was said: By life is meant fertility and by death drought. It was said: He makes sleep and wakes. It was said: He causes death in this world and gives life for the Resurrection.

﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾, meaning from the offspring of Adam; He does not mean Adam and Eve, that they were created from a drop.

The nutfah is little water, derived from nataffa al-ma' idha qatar (the water dripped).

﴿Emitted (tumna)﴾ means poured into the womb and spilled. This was said by al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak and Ata ibn Abi Rabah. It is said: manā al-rajul and amnā from al-maniyy (semen). Mina was named by this name because blood is poured (yumna) there, meaning shed. It was said: (tumna) means is measured out; this was said by Abu Ubayda. It is said: manaytu al-shay' idha qaddartuhu (I measured the thing when I determined it), and muniya lahu meaning it was decreed for him. The poet said [[Its speaker is Abu Qilabah al-Hudhali. Its first half:

"And do not say to a thing, 'I will surely do it'"

It is also said it belongs to Suwayd ibn Amir al-Mustaliqi. Before it:

"Do not feel safe from death in a sanctuary or outside it, for the appointed fates reach every person,
and take your path therein without shame..." until...]]:

"Until you meet what the Measurer has measured for you."

That is, what the one who decrees has decreed for you.

Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life...﴾ [[See vol. 7 p. 78 and vol. 6 p. 418]], the verse. It was said: He causes the drop to die and gives life to the soul. It was said: He causes the fathers to die and gives life to the sons. It was said: By life is meant fertility and by death drought. It was said: He makes sleep and wakes. It was said: He causes death in this world and gives life for the Resurrection.

﴿And that He created the pairs, the male and the female﴾, meaning from the offspring of Adam; He does not mean Adam and Eve, that they were created from a drop.

The nutfah is little water, derived from nataffa al-ma' idha qatar (the water dripped).

﴿Emitted (tumna)﴾ means poured into the womb and spilled. This was said by al-Kalbi, al-Dahhak and Ata ibn Abi Rabah. It is said: manā al-rajul and amnā from al-maniyy (semen). It is said: manaytu al-shay' idha qaddartuhu (I measured the thing when I determined it), and muniya lahu meaning it was decreed for him. The poet said [[Its speaker is Abu Qilabah al-Hudhali. Its first half:

It is also said it belongs to Suwayd ibn Amir al-Mustaliqi. Before it:

"Do not feel safe from death in a sanctuary or outside it, for the appointed fates reach every person,
and take your path therein without shame..." until...]]:

"Until you meet what the Measurer has measured for you."

That is, what the one who decrees has decreed for you.

Then he recited: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 307]. He also recited: ﴿Allah withholds and extends﴾ [See vol. 3, p. 237], and al-Tabari preferred this view. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan that (aghna) means he made wealthy (mawwala), and (aqna) means he made [people] to have servants (akhdama). It was said that (aqna) means He made for you property (qinyah) that you possess, which also means "made to have servants." It was also said that its meaning is "He made [him] content with what He gave," i.e., He made him rich and then made him content with what He had given him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Jawhari said: "qana al-rajulu yaqna qina, like ghina yaghna ghina, and Allah aqnahu," meaning Allah gave him what is possessed as property (qinyah) and wealth (nashab). "Aqnahu Allah" also means "He made him content." Al-qina means contentment, according to Abu Zayd, who said: The Arabs say, "Whoever is given a hundred goats has been given qina; whoever is given a hundred sheep has been given ghina; whoever is given a hundred camels has been given muna." It is also said: "Allah aghnahu and aqnahu," meaning He gave him what he could rely on. It was said: (aghna wa aqna) means He made himself rich and made his creation needy of Him, as said by Sulayman al-Taymi. Sufyan said: He made [him] rich through contentment and made [him] content through satisfaction. Al-Akhfash said: (aqna) means "made poor." Ibn Kaysan said: "He made [him] have children." This returns to what was mentioned earlier.

﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of Sirius﴾. Al-Shi'ra (Sirius) is the bright star that rises after al-Jawza' (Orion), and its rising occurs in the intensity of heat. There are two Sirii: al-Sha'ra al-'Abur, which is in al-Jawza', and al-Sha'ra al-Ghumaysa', which is in al-Dhira'. The Arabs claim that they are the two sisters of Suhayl (Canopus). The reason it is mentioned that He is the Lord of Sirius, even though He is the Lord of everything, is that the Arabs used to worship it, so Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed them that Sirius is something created (marbub) and not a lord (rabb). There is disagreement about who worshipped it. Al-Suddi said: Himyar and Khuza'ah used to worship it. Others said: The first to worship it was Abu Kabshah, one of the maternal ancestors of the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason, the polytheists of Quraysh would call the Prophet (ﷺ) "the son of Abu Kabshah" when he called to Allah and opposed their religions, and they would say: "What we have met from the son of Abu Kabshah!" Abu Sufyan said on the day of the Conquest, when he stood in one of the narrow passes while the armies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by him: "Indeed the affair of the son of Abu Kabshah has become mighty." Even among the Arabs who did not worship Sirius, they used to revere it and believe in its influence on the world. The poet said:

*Ayloul has passed and the scorching heat has risen,*
*and al-Sha'ra al-'Abur has extinguished its fire.*

It was also said that the Arabs say in their myths: Suhayl and al-Sha'ra were a married couple. Suhayl descended and became Yemeni, so al-Sha'ra al-'Abur followed him and crossed the Milky Way, and so she was called al-'Abur (the one who crosses). Al-Ghumaysa' remained behind and wept for the loss of Suhayl until her eyes became inflamed (ghumisat), so she was named al-Ghumaysa' because she is less bright than the other.

﴿And that it was He who destroyed the first 'Ad﴾. He called them "the first" because they were from before Thamud. It was said: Thamud were from the lineage (min nasl) of 'Ad. Ibn Zayd said: It was called "the first 'Ad" because it was the first nation destroyed after Nuh (peace be upon him). Ibn Ishaq said: There were two 'Ad: the first was destroyed by the violent wind, and then the second was destroyed by the Cry. It was said: The first 'Ad is 'Ad son of Iram son of 'Aws son of Sam son of Nuh, and the second 'Ad are descendants of the first 'Ad; the meanings are close. It was also said: The last 'Ad are the tyrants, and they are the people of Hud.

The common recitation is (' Adan al-ula) with clear tanwin (nunation) and hamza. Nafi', Ibn Muhaysin and Abu 'Amr recited (' Adan al-ula) by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the lam and merging the tanwin into it, except that Qalun and al-Susi pronounce the sukun hamza clearly. The rest changed it to a waw in accordance with its origin. The Arabs make this change, saying: "Qum al-an 'anna" and "wa dumm li-thnayn," meaning "Qum al-an wa dumm al-ithnayn" [stand up now and gather the two].

﴿And Thamud, He spared none﴾. Thamud were the people of Salih, who were destroyed by the Cry. It is recited (Thamudan) and (wa Thamuda), which has already been discussed [See vol. 7, p. 238]. It is in the accusative as a conjunction with 'Ad.

﴿And the people of Nuh before them﴾, i.e., He also destroyed the people of Nuh before 'Ad and Thamud. ﴿Indeed they were more wrongful and more rebellious﴾. This was due to the long duration of Nuh's stay among them, to the point that a man would take his son by the hand and go to Nuh (peace be upon him) and say: "Beware of this one, for he is a liar, and my father walked with me to this man and said to me what I say to you." So the elder would die upon disbelief, and the young would grow up upon the advice of his father. It was also said: The pronoun refers to all those mentioned of 'Ad, Thamud and the people of Nuh, i.e., they were more disbelieving than the polytheists of the Arabs and more rebellious. This contains consolation and comfort for the Prophet (ﷺ), as if He were saying to him: "So be patient, you too, for the praiseworthy end will be yours."

﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down﴾. This refers to the cities of the people of Lut (peace be upon him), which were overturned upon them, i.e., turned upside down so that their upper part became their lower part. It is said: "afakatuhu," meaning I turned him over and changed him.

(Ahwa): i.e., they were sunk after being raised to the sky. Jibril raised them and then brought them down to the earth. Al-Mubarrad said: He made them fall. It is said: "hawa" with a fatha, yahwi hawiyan, meaning fell, and (ahwa) means "made to fall."

﴿Then He covered them with what covered them﴾, i.e., He clothed them with the stones that clothed them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of hard clay﴾ [See vol. 10, p. 542]. It was also said: The pronoun refers to all these nations, i.e., He covered them with the punishment that covered them, and it is left vague because each of them was destroyed by a different kind [of punishment] from the others. It was also said: This is to magnify the matter.

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you dispute?﴾, i.e., about which of the blessings of your Lord do you doubt? The address is to the denying human being. Al-ala' (favours) are blessings; their singular forms are alan, ilan and ilin. Ya'qub recited (tamara) by merging one of the two taa' into the other with shaddah.

**Tafsir of verse 47–55:**

Allah's words: ﴿And that unto your Lord is the final destination﴾, which is to say, the returning of the spirits into bodies for the Resurrection. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited (al-nash'ah) with a fatha on the shin and a long vowel (madd), meaning: He promised this, and His promise is true.

﴿And that it is He who makes rich and gives contentment﴾. Ibn Zayd said: He makes rich whom He wills and makes poor whom He wills. Then he recited: ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it for him﴾ [See vol. 14, p. 307]. He also recited: ﴿Allah withholds and extends﴾ [See vol. 3, p. 237], and al-Tabari preferred this view. It is also reported from Ibn Zayd, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Hasan that (aghna) means he made wealthy (mawwala), and (aqna) means he made [people] to have servants (akhdama). It was said that (aqna) means He made for you property (qinyah) that you possess, which also means "made to have servants." It was also said that its meaning is "He made [him] content with what He gave," i.e., He made him rich and then made him content with what He had given him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Jawhari said: "qana al-rajulu yaqna qina, like ghina yaghna ghina, and Allah aqnahu," meaning Allah gave him what is possessed as property (qinyah) and wealth (nashab). "Aqnahu Allah" also means "He made him content." Al-qina means contentment, according to Abu Zayd, who said: The Arabs say, "Whoever is given a hundred goats has been given qina; whoever is given a hundred sheep has been given ghina; whoever is given a hundred camels has been given muna." It is also said: "Allah aghnahu and aqnahu," meaning He gave him what he could rely on. It was said: (aghna wa aqna) means He made himself rich and made his creation needy of Him, as said by Sulayman al-Taymi. Sufyan said: He made [him] rich through contentment and made [him] content through satisfaction. Al-Akhfash said: (aqna) means "made poor." Ibn Kaysan said: "He made [him] have children." This returns to what was mentioned earlier.

﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of Sirius﴾. Al-Shi'ra (Sirius) is the bright star that rises after al-Jawza' (Orion), and its rising occurs in the intensity of heat. There are two Sirii: al-Sha'ra al-'Abur, which is in al-Jawza', and al-Sha'ra al-Ghumaysa', which is in al-Dhira'. The Arabs claim that they are the two sisters of Suhayl (Canopus). *Ayloul has passed and the scorching heat has risen,*
*and al-Sha'ra al-'Abur has extinguished its fire.*

It was also said that the Arabs say in their myths: Suhayl and al-Sha'ra were a married couple. Al-Ghumaysa' remained behind and wept for the loss of Suhayl until her eyes became inflamed (ghumisat), so she was named al-Ghumaysa' because she is less bright than the other.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 53, verses 56–62:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is a warner of the warnings of old﴾. Ibn Juraij and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: He means that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a warner with the truth with which the prophets before him warned. If you obey him, you will prosper; otherwise, there will befall you what befell the deniers of the earlier messengers. Qatadah said: He means the Qur'an, and that it is a warner with what the earlier scriptures warned of. It was also said: That is, what We have told you of the news of the past nations who were destroyed is a warning to this community, lest there befall them what befell those (nations). "Nudhur" (warnings) means "mithl al-nudhur" (like the warnings). In the speech of the Arabs, "nudhur" carries the meaning of "indhar" (warning), as "nukur" carries the meaning of "inkar" (denial); that is, "This is a warning to you." Abu Malik said: What I have warned you of, of the events of the bygone nations, is in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa. Al-Suddi said: Abu Salih informed me, saying: These are the words which Allah mentioned from His saying: (Has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Musa and Ibrahim) up to His saying: (This is a warner of the warnings of old), all of this is in the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾, that is, the Hour has come near and the Resurrection has approached. He named it "the Imminent" (āzifah) because of the nearness of its establishment to Him, as He said: (They see it as distant, but We see it as near) [See vol. 18, p. 284]. It was also said: He named it "the Imminent" because of its approach to people and its nearness to them, so that they might prepare for it, for everything that is coming is near. The poet said:

The departure has drawn near, but our riding-camels
have not yet been loaded with our saddles, as if it had already come.

In al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "azifa al-tarahhul" means it drew near and approached, and from this is His saying: ﴿The Imminent Event has drawn near﴾, meaning the Resurrection. "Azifa al-rajulu" means he hastened; so he is "āzif" in the form of "fā'il." "Al-mutāzif" is the short one, who is close (to others). Abu Zayd said: I asked a Bedouin, "What is al-muhbanti'?" He said, "The one who is hurried." I said, "What is al-mutakakki'?" He said, "The one who is hurried." I said, "What is al-mutāzif?" He said, "You are a fool," and he left me and passed on.

(There is no one to reveal it besides Allah): that is, there is no one besides Allah who can delay it or hasten it. It was also said: "Kāshifah" means "inkishāf" (disclosure); that is, none reveals it or manifests it except Allah. So "al-kāshifah" is a noun with the meaning of a verbal noun, and the "ha'" in it is like the "ha'" in "al-'āqibah," "al-'āfiyah," "al-dāhiyah" and "al-bāqiyah," as in the saying: "mā li-fulān min bāqiyah" (Fulan has no remainder), meaning no survival. It was also said: That is, none can avert it; namely, when the Resurrection comes, none of their gods can reveal it, and none besides Allah, Exalted is He, can save them. The Resurrection has been named "the Overwhelming" (ghāshiyah), and when it is an overwhelming (event), its averting is a disclosure. So "al-kāshifah" on this view is an adjective of a feminine noun that is omitted, meaning "nafs kāshifah" (a soul that discloses), or "firqah kāshifah" (a group that discloses), or "hāl kāshifah" (a state that discloses). It was also said: "Kāshifah" means "kāshif" (the one who discloses), and the "ha'" is for emphasis, like "rāwiyah" and "dāhiyah."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do you then wonder at this discourse?﴾ meaning the Qur'an. This is a rebuke-question. (And you laugh) in denial of it, (and do not weep) out of fear and dread of the threat. It is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ), after the revelation of this verse, was not seen laughing except with a smile. Abu Hurairah said: When (Do you then wonder at this discourse?) was revealed, the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Suffah) said: "Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return," and then they wept until their tears flowed upon their cheeks. When the Prophet (ﷺ) heard their weeping, he wept with them, and we wept at his weeping. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No one who weeps out of the fear of Allah will enter the Fire, and no one who persists in disobedience to Allah will enter Paradise. Had you not sinned, Allah would have taken you away and brought a people who sin, and He would forgive them and have mercy upon them; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Abu Hazim said: Jibril descended upon the Prophet (ﷺ) while there was a man with him who was weeping. He said to him: "Who is this?" He (the Prophet) said: "This is so-and-so." Jibril said: "We weigh all the deeds of the children of Adam except weeping, for indeed Allah extinguishes with a single tear seas of Hellfire."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you are sāmidūn﴾, that is, heedless and turning away. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, transmitted by al-Walibi and al-'Awfi from him. 'Ikrimah said, from him: It is singing in the language of Himyar; it is said, "Sammid lanā," meaning "sing for us." So when they heard the Qur'an being recited, they would sing and play until they could not hear it. Al-Dahhak said: "Sāmidūn" means proud and arrogant. In al-Sihah: "Samada sumūdan" means he raised his head in arrogance, and every one who raises his head is "sāmid." The poet said:

Sawāmid al-layl, light in their provisions.

He means: there is no fodder in their bellies. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Samadtu sumūdan" means I rose high. "Samadat al-ibil fī sayrihā" means the camels pressed on in their journey. "Al-sumūd" is amusement, and "al-sāmid" is the one who is amused. It is said to the singing-girl, "Asmidīnā," meaning "Entertain us with singing." "Tasmīd al-ard" means putting "al-simād" in it, which is dung and ash. "Tasmīd al-ra's" means shaving its hair, a dialectal variant of "tasbīd." "Isma'adda al-rajulu" with a hamzah means he swelled up in anger. It is reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that the meaning of "sāmidūn" is that they sit without praying or awaiting prayer. Al-Hasan said: They stand for prayer before the imam stands. From this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he went out and found people standing, waiting for him, and he said: "What is wrong with you that I see you as sāmidūn?" Al-Mawardi related this. Al-Mahdawi mentioned it from 'Ali, that he went out to prayer and saw people standing waiting for him, and he said: "What is wrong with you, sāmidūn?" Al-Mahdawi related this. The well-known usage in the language is: "samada yasmudu sumūdan" when he amused himself and turned away. Al-Mubarrad said: "Sāmidūn" means "khāmidūn" (languid). The poet said:

Misfortune came upon the women of the family of Harb
with a decree they were languid for.

Salih Abu al-Khalil said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Do you then wonder at this discourse? And you laugh and do not weep? And you are sāmidūn), he was not seen laughing except smiling, until he died (ﷺ). Al-Nahhas related this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship﴾. It is said: The intended meaning is the prostration of recitation of the Qur'an. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i held it. It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in it and the polytheists prostrated with him. It was said: The polytheists prostrated with him only because they heard the voices of the devils during the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at his saying: (Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other one?), and that he said: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is hoped for." This is in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr ("turtaja" — is hoped for). In the narration of Abu al-'Aliyah it is ("turtada" — is approved), and "such as they are not forgotten." The polytheists rejoiced and thought that it was from the words of Muhammad (ﷺ), as has already been explained in (al-Hajj) [[These reports are among the fabrications against the infallible master of creation, peace be upon him, and it is impossible that he should utter what contradicts the Qur'an, or that Satan should speak through his tongue. Everything of this kind is false, fabricated by heretics to gain entry into slandering our master Muhammad (ﷺ) or the revelation, or the Qur'an, which he does not speak from desire. See what the author wrote about this hadith in vol. 12, p. 80.]]. When the news reached those of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were in Abyssinia, they returned, thinking that the people of Makkah had embraced Islam. Then the people of Makkah became harsher against them and began to torment them, until Allah lifted that from them. It was also said: The intended meaning is the obligatory prostration in prayer. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and you are sāmidūn﴾, that is, heedless and turning away. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, transmitted by al-Walibi and al-'Awfi from him. 'Ikrimah said, from him: It is singing in the language of Himyar; it is said, "Sammid lanā," meaning "sing for us." So when they heard the Qur'an being recited, they would sing and play until they could not hear it. Al-Dahhak said: "Sāmidūn" means proud and arrogant. In al-Sihah: "Samada sumūdan" means he raised his head in arrogance, and every one who raises his head is "sāmid." The poet said:

Sawāmid al-layl, light in their provisions.

He means: there is no fodder in their bellies. Ibn al-A'rabi said: "Samadtu sumūdan" means I rose high. "Samadat al-ibil fī sayrihā" means the camels pressed on in their journey. "Al-sumūd" is amusement, and "al-sāmid" is the one who is amused. It is said to the singing-girl, "Asmidīnā," meaning "Entertain us with singing." "Tasmīd al-ard" means putting "al-simād" in it, which is dung and ash. "Tasmīd al-ra's" means shaving its hair, a dialectal variant of "tasbīd." "Isma'adda al-rajulu" with a hamzah means he swelled up in anger. It is reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that the meaning of "sāmidūn" is that they sit without praying or awaiting prayer. Al-Hasan said: They stand for prayer before the imam stands. From this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he went out and found people standing, waiting for him, and he said: "What is wrong with you that I see you as sāmidūn?" Al-Mawardi related this. Al-Mahdawi mentioned it from 'Ali, that he went out to prayer and saw people standing waiting for him, and he said: "What is wrong with you, sāmidūn?" Al-Mahdawi related this. The well-known usage in the language is: "samada yasmudu sumūdan" when he amused himself and turned away. Al-Mubarrad said: "Sāmidūn" means "khāmidūn" (languid). The poet said:

Misfortune came upon the women of the family of Harb
with a decree they were languid for.

Salih Abu al-Khalil said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited (Do you then wonder at this discourse? And you laugh and do not weep? And you are sāmidūn), he was not seen laughing except smiling, until he died (ﷺ). Al-Nahhas related this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So prostrate to Allah and worship﴾. It is said: The intended meaning is the prostration of recitation of the Qur'an. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, and Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i held it. It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah, from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in it and the polytheists prostrated with him. It was said: The polytheists prostrated with him only because they heard the voices of the devils during the recitation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at his saying: (Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other one?), and that he said: "Those are the exalted cranes, and their intercession is hoped for." This is in the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr ("turtaja" — is hoped for). In the narration of Abu al-'Aliyah it is ("turtada" — is approved), and "such as they are not forgotten." The polytheists rejoiced and thought that it was from the words of Muhammad (ﷺ), as has already been explained in (al-Hajj) [[These reports are among the fabrications against the infallible master of creation, peace be upon him, and it is impossible that he should utter what contradicts the Qur'an, or that Satan should speak through his tongue. Everything of this kind is false, fabricated by heretics to gain entry into slandering our master Muhammad (ﷺ) or the revelation, or the Qur'an, which he does not speak from desire. See what the author wrote about this hadith in vol. 12, p. 80.]]. When the news reached those of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were in Abyssinia, they returned, thinking that the people of Makkah had embraced Islam. Then the people of Makkah became harsher against them and began to torment them, until Allah lifted that from them. It was also said: The intended meaning is the obligatory prostration in prayer. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar, who did not regard it as one of the obligatory prostrations. Malik also held this view. Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: The last action of the Prophet (ﷺ) was leaving off prostration in al-Mufassal. The first view is more sound, and the discussion of it has already passed, explained at the end of (al-A'raf) [See vol. 7, p. 357]. And praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The commentary of the Surah (al-Najm) is complete.
